During the same session, Azerbaijan’s representative remained in the hall while Netanyahu delivered a speech in which he called Erdoğan a “tyrant”.

— Speaking at the UN General Assembly, Erdoğan described bans on headscarves in schools in “some countries” as an infringement of women’s rights. During the same session, Azerbaijan’s representative remained in the hall while Netanyahu delivered a speech in which he called Erdoğan a “tyrant”. 2 October — Speaking at a congress of the ruling New Azerbaijan Party (YAP), Aliyev said, without naming anyone in particular, that everyone should “know their place” and that nobody had the right to interfere in the Azerbaijani people’s way of life. He stressed that Azerbaijan had achieved its military victories without foreign patronage and had bought weapons with its own money (JAMnews).

— Speaking at a congress of the ruling New Azerbaijan Party (YAP), Aliyev said, without naming anyone in particular, that everyone should “know their place” and that nobody had the right to interfere in the Azerbaijani people’s way of life. He stressed that Azerbaijan had achieved its military victories without foreign patronage and had bought weapons with its own money (JAMnews). 9–12 October — Azerbaijani schools began inspections during which officials barred female pupils and teachers wearing hijabs from attending classes. The measures sparked protests and led to the detention of 37 people (JAMnews).

— Azerbaijani schools began inspections during which officials barred female pupils and teachers wearing hijabs from attending classes. The measures sparked protests and led to the detention of 37 people (JAMnews). 12 October — Erdoğan’s chief adviser Oktay Saral called on Azerbaijan to “correct this mistake” as soon as possible. Leyla Şahin Usta, deputy chair of the parliamentary group of the Justice and Development Party (AKP), made a similar statement.

— Erdoğan’s chief adviser Oktay Saral called on Azerbaijan to “correct this mistake” as soon as possible. Leyla Şahin Usta, deputy chair of the parliamentary group of the Justice and Development Party (AKP), made a similar statement. 13 October — YAP’s press service criticised Saral and AKP MPs, naming them individually. Its statement called on the AKP to abandon its “harmful policy” and also referred to “hegemonic ambitions” (Yeni Azerbaijan).

— YAP’s press service criticised Saral and AKP MPs, naming them individually. Its statement called on the AKP to abandon its “harmful policy” and also referred to “hegemonic ambitions” (Yeni Azerbaijan). 14–15 October — Fidan arrived in Baku and met Aliyev.

Against this backdrop, AKP spokesperson Ömer Çelik limited his response to saying that the two countries’ leaders shared a “genuinely brotherly relationship”.

Why relations are cooling: Israel, Russia and claims to the role of “big brother”

All the experts JAMnews interviewed before Fidan’s visit believe the hijab issue represents just one manifestation of deeper problems in relations between Azerbaijan and Turkey.

“The need to choose between two rivals”

Araz Aliyev | Photo: Third Republic Platform

Politician Araz Aliyev, one of the founders of the Third Republic Platform, told JAMnews that he linked the current tensions to Azerbaijan’s foreign policy.

In his view, Baku has begun to see itself as “a major geopolitical player”. However, unlike the US or China, Azerbaijan lacks the capacity to maintain close relations with two rival states at the same time:

“Over the next ten years, Turkey and Israel will be the two main rivals in the Middle East. At the same time, Azerbaijan is a strategic ally of both countries. When Netanyahu speaks, the Turkish delegation leaves the hall, while the Azerbaijani delegation cannot do the same, even if it wants to. Israel also invests in Azerbaijan and supports it. Naturally, this causes resentment in Turkey.”

Araz Aliyev notes that Azerbaijan first felt the negative consequences of its “multi-vector policy” after it backed Pakistan in its confrontation with India. According to the politician, India blocked Azerbaijan’s accession to the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation, while trade between the two countries — worth as much as $2 billion — suffered a setback.

Aliyev identifies Russia as a second factor. In his view, Baku has been pursuing closer relations with Moscow since August. He sees the resolution of disagreements over the crash of an AZAL aircraft as one sign of this rapprochement. Historically, he notes, closer ties between Azerbaijan and Russia have gone hand in hand with a degree of distancing from Turkey.

Araz Aliyev also links these changes to the domestic political situation in the US. In his view, Baku’s foreign policy strategy, which has largely relied on Donald Trump’s administration, could come under threat if Republicans lose the US midterm elections in November. The politician believes concerns about this scenario are pushing the Azerbaijani authorities to seek alternative foreign policy partners.

“I don’t depend on you”

Ömer Faruk Gergerlioğlu | Photo: Grand National Assembly of Turkey

Ömer Faruk Gergerlioğlu, a member of Turkey’s parliament representing Kocaeli province and the Peoples’ Equality and Democracy Party (DEM), told JAMnews that he sees Aliyev’s 2 October speech as a rejection of Turkey’s claim to the role of “big brother”.

“Turkey has always seen itself as the big brother of Central Asian countries and Azerbaijan. Aliyev, however, disagrees. His message is: I don’t depend on you; I need you only as much as you need me. We have mutual interests, but ours is not a relationship between an older and a younger brother.”

In the MP’s view, Baku sees cooperation with Israel as a “lifeline” that helps it preserve its authoritarian system of government, and it has no intention of making concessions on this issue.

Gergerlioğlu also points to what he sees as contradictions in Erdoğan’s position. The Turkish president sharply criticises Israel but turns a blind eye to oil shipments from the Turkish port of Ceyhan to Israel. The oil reaches the port through the Baku-Tbilisi-Ceyhan pipeline. The MP claims he has repeatedly presented the government with documentary evidence of these shipments.

“If tensions between Turkey and Israel escalate, I think Aliyev will openly side with Israel. For him, the principle of ‘one nation, two states’ takes a back seat. He views the world primarily through the lens of preserving his own power.”

Against this backdrop, Fidan’s decision to walk out rather than listen to Israeli President Isaac Herzog’s speech in Baku takes on particular significance. This time, Ankara demonstrated its differences with Azerbaijan over Israel directly in the Azerbaijani capital.

Growing discontent in Turkish society

Джавид Ага | Фото: личный архив

Journalist and analyst Javid Agha notes that discontent with Azerbaijan in Turkish society extends beyond the hijab issue.

According to him, Turkish businesspeople have complained for years about the difficulties of doing business in Azerbaijan, demands for unofficial payments by tax authorities and deliberate delays affecting lorries at the Georgian-Azerbaijani border.

“Turkish society has accumulated numerous grievances against Azerbaijan. However, people have only begun expressing them more openly and actively since the summer. Previously, Erdoğan’s inner circle kept this discontent in check through groups it funded, which fell silent at the president’s first signal. Now I see posts supporting protests in Azerbaijan on Instagram, TikTok and even platforms where I would never have imagined seeing such things before.”

The hijab factor: a sensitive issue for Turkey

The de facto ban on wearing the hijab in Azerbaijani schools has provoked a particularly strong reaction in Turkey. According to Gergerlioğlu, bans on headscarves remained one of the most hotly debated issues in Turkish society from the 1980s until the 2010s. Today, even voters who support the secular Republican People’s Party (CHP) consider the issue “a thing of the past”.

“Footage showing girls in headscarves being turned away from school brings back painful memories for Turkish society. Supporters of the ban argued that without it, Turkey would become a state governed by Sharia law. But the ban was lifted, and Turkey still did not become a Sharia state.”

The MP also clashed with Azerbaijani lawmakers over the issue. He said that during an online meeting of the Parliamentary Assembly of Turkic States (TURKPA), he criticised the ban. Azerbaijani MP Hikmet Mammadov then claimed that no such ban existed in the country and accused him of lying. However, according to Gergerlioğlu, a lawmaker from Turkey’s ruling Justice and Development Party (AKP), who attended the meeting, chose to remain silent.

Araz Aliyev believes Ankara’s reaction was inevitable. In his view, under Erdoğan, Turkey presents itself as a defender of “moderate Islam” and Muslims, while religious voters form one of the ruling party’s main support bases. “In this situation, Baku’s decision could not go unanswered,” he says.

Javid Agha, meanwhile, points out that Leyla Şahin Usta was among those whom Azerbaijan’s ruling New Azerbaijan Party (YAP) criticised in its statement. In the late 1990s, a headscarf ban prevented her from continuing her studies in Istanbul. Şahin Usta later lost her case against Turkey at the European Court of Human Rights and completed her education in Vienna.

“These bans did not stop her. Today, she is among those who govern Turkey. The authors of the statement should at least have familiarised themselves with her biography,” Agha says.

Sheikh-ul-Islam: “Consultations could have taken place, but they did not”

Allahshukur Pashazade, chairman of the Caucasus Muslims Board, has also commented on the situation. In an interview with Real TV, he acknowledged that the authorities had not consulted the religious organisation he heads before making the decision:

“I deeply regret that consultations could have taken place on this issue in advance, but they did not.”

At the same time, Pashazade supported the government’s position. He said the school uniform regulations do not mention the word “hijab” and that the country has no ban on wearing it. Children can study in hijabs at madrasas, he added, “but a different decision was taken regarding state schools”.

The Sheikh-ul-Islam stressed that “religion is separate from the state, and school is separate from religion”. He also accused certain “internal and external forces” of politicising the issue and trying to turn citizens against the state.

Araz Aliyev sees Pashazade’s statement as evidence that the authorities made the decision hastily:

“If the decision had been carefully considered and prepared over many years, the authorities should have consulted someone. It appears they made the decision in haste.”

For more on the legal aspects of the hijab ban, protests at schools and detentions, see JAMnews’ earlier report.

How will relations develop?

None of the experts interviewed expects Azerbaijan and Turkey to break off their alliance. However, they all believe the chill between the two countries will persist for some time.

Araz Aliyev believes the tensions will remain at the political level and gradually ease:

“Turkey needs Azerbaijan, while Azerbaijan needs Turkey even more in terms of national security, the economy and defence. Companies close to the leadership in both countries may face pressure from one another, but I do not believe their alliance will be threatened. After some time, we will hear declarations of brotherhood again.”

He notes that the two countries have weathered similar crises in the past. In particular, tensions in the late 2000s, when Turkey and Armenia were discussing protocols to normalise relations, led to Turkish flags being taken down in Baku. Aliyev believes the summit of the Organisation of Turkic States, which is expected to take place in Turkey at the end of the month, could indicate the direction in which relations between Baku and Ankara will develop.

Gergerlioğlu also does not expect Erdoğan to distance himself from Baku solely over the hijab issue. He says Ankara places much greater importance on revenue from the Baku-Tbilisi-Ceyhan pipeline, Turkey’s ambition to play a leading role in the “Turkic world” and the support of its nationalist-conservative electorate.

“Behind closed doors, they will probably say politely: ‘Wouldn’t it have been better not to introduce such a ban?’ However, if Aliyev begins openly supporting Israel, Turkey will also start signalling its discontent with the relationship more openly.”

The MP also points to declining electoral support for the ruling party. He claims that some voters dissatisfied with the AKP’s “two-faced” policy towards Israel backed the New Welfare Party in the last election. In his view, the hijab issue could deepen this discontent further.

Javid Agha reaches a similar conclusion. He believes that no matter how often Erdoğan repeats the slogan “one nation, two states”, he will have to take into account the views of the religious-conservative electorate that forms the foundation of his political support and adjust his position accordingly.

Fidan’s statements in Baku also offer insight into this diplomatic strategy. Ankara does not deny that problems exist, but seeks to move discussions about them out of the public arena and into closed-door diplomatic channels. So far, however, there are no signs that Baku intends to make concessions either on the hijab issue or on its relations with Israel.

Strained relations between Turkey and Azerbaijan

World.title: Chronicles of Victory: October 18, 2020
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 18. The Azerbaijani Army launched a counter-offensive operation, later called the "Iron Fist", on September 27, 2020, in response to the large-scale provocation of the Armenian armed forces along the frontline.

The 44-day second Karabakh war ended with the liberation of Azerbaijan’s territories from nearly 30-year Armenian occupation and the restoration of territorial integrity.

Trend presents the chronicle of the 22nd day of the Second Karabakh war:

- A publication about the Azerbaijani Armed Forces raising the Azerbaijani flag over the ancient Khudafarin bridge was posted on the official Twitter page of the President of Azerbaijan Ilham Aliyev.

- First Vice-President of the Republic of Azerbaijan Mehriban Aliyeva has made a post on her official Instagram page.

- Despite the announcement of a new humanitarian ceasefire, the Armenian armed forces once again grossly violated the agreement.

- The Ministry of Defense of Azerbaijan has published a list of destroyed enemy equipment and announced the capture of an Armenian military unit.

- The Air Defense Units of Azerbaijan shot down another Su-25 attack aircraft of the Armenian Armed Forces.

- Armenian armed forces attempted to attack in Aghdara, Fuzuli, Hadrut, and Jabrayil directions.

- Azerbaijani soldiers captured positions of Armenian special forces. Another tactical UAV of Armenia was destroyed.

- The Azerbaijani Defense Ministry announced the seizure of military equipment and ammunition of the Armenian Armed Forces.

- Azerbaijani flag was raised in center of liberated from occupation Fuzuli city.

BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 17. Azerbaijani judokas won a total of 8 medals, including 4 silver and 4 bronze, on the first day of the Aktau Asian Open, the Azerbaijan Judo Federation said.

Nazim Talibov (66 kg), Kamran Suleymanov (73 kg), Farida Mirzoyeva (52 kg) and Ulviya Bayramova (57 kg) reached the finals and claimed silver medals.

World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 17. Average prices for Azeri Light (CIF), Azeri Light (FOB Ceyhan), Dated Brent, and Urals crude decreased from October 12 through October 16.

According to Trend’s calculations, based on data from oil market participants, the average price of Azeri Light (CIF) crude, produced at the Azeri-Chirag-Guneshli field in Azerbaijan, decreased by $3.1, or 2.4%, compared to the previous week, reaching $123.79 per barrel.

Dated Brent crude averaged $126.98 per barrel, down $2.96, or 2.3%, from the previous week. During the week, the price reached a high of $134.25 per barrel and a low of $116.59.

World.title: Back where they belong, Murray Cod bring new life to SA's Lake Bonney
World.content:
A freshwater lake is hoped to become a thriving ecosystem after hundreds of mature native Murray Cod were reintroduced to its waters for the first time in years.

Around 600 cod were returned to Lake Bonney, which is connected to the River Murray, in South Australia's Riverland last week.

It was a project driven by Recfish SA and backed by the state government and its newly established Recreational Fishing Authority.

RecFish SA chief executive Asher Dezsery said it was a significant moment to see cod enter the water, as populations had died out from the lake many years prior.

RecFish SA's Asher Dezsery was proud to lead the reintroduction of the Murray Cod at Lake Bonney. (ABC Riverland: Oliver Brown)

"Throughout various water quality issues, the lake got segregated from the river, and unfortunately there were a few fish kills here that removed all of the cod," he said.

"These are big fish, they're not fingerlings, these are up to a metre.

"They're going to be instant broodstock [mature individuals specifically used for breeding], creating an instant fishery to push recreational fishing tourism in this area."

RecFish SA Riverland board member Lucas Weaver says it is a "dream come true" for locals to return Murray Cod to Lake Bonney. (ABC Riverland: Oliver Brown)

New natives to improve ecosystem

Charles Sturt University's Paul Humphries said cod defined the Murray-Darling Basin and its connected systems.

"They will improve generally the water, the structure and the water quality, because they actually are, to a degree, habitat engineers," the ecology associate professor said.

Fish ecologist Paul Humphries welcomes any effort to increase the number of Murray Cod in the system. (Supplied: Paul Humphries)

Dr Humphries also said cod played a major role in the natural food chain, but was not certain they would make a dent in the large carp population.

"If there's small fish around, like carp, they'll certainly have a go at them. [But] cod tend to be main channel specialists," he said.

"Carp are such prolific breeders. It's not something that can be solved very easily by just throwing a few hundred cod in, but it certainly can't hurt."

For Ngintait elder Norman Wilson, the lake and the Murray Cod are culturally significant.

He said he hoped some of the fish would migrate into the river system but believed they would return to breed.

Ngintait elder Norman Wilson and River Murray and Mallee Aboriginal Corporation director Sarah Lindsay enjoyed taking part in the cod release. (ABC Riverland: Oliver Brown)

"That's their cycle; they'll always come back to the same place [so] there's going to be cod here at all times," he said.

Council hopeful for tourism boost

Berri Barmera Council mayor Ella Winnall was among the locals who helped return the native cod to Lake Bonney at a special event in early October.

She said it was a "once in a lifetime opportunity" to be up close with so many mature cod, giving locals and visitors another reason to spend time at the lake.

State recreation minister Rhiannon Pearce, Barmera resident Shila Giles and Berri Barmera mayor Ella Winnall all helped with the cod releases. (ABC Riverland: Oliver Brown)

"There aren't many people in the community that don't have a rod and reel in the shed or a boat licence," Ms Winnall said.

"This just adds another element of people wanting to come to Lake Bonney and Barmera to catch the cod."

Fishing for Murray Cod is not allowed during the breeding season, but South Australia's catch-and-release season resumes from January 1, 2027.

World.title: A secret diagnosis could have torn us apart, but it brought us together
World.content:
When Vinko Anthony finally got the courage to tell the love of his life a secret he had been hiding for five years, he had to trust the love and listening he'd given Andrea Zara in the relationship would be gracefully given back to him.

Whether it's romantic, platonic, heartbreaking or surprising, our Love Story series is about love in all its forms. Share yours with us.

These are Vinko and Andrea's words.

There were 20,000 people and there he was

Vinko: In 2010, I was living in Sydney and decided to go on a European holiday.

I was in Dubrovnik; Croatia one morning swimming after doing yoga and I looked up and there was this cuteness overload standing there dancing naked on a rock with no music on and I went, "Oh my God."

It sounds like it was sexual, but it wasn't, it was more Andrea's joy and that someone would have a free spirit to do something like that, he was just having a great time.

Andrea has always and will always have this childlike, curious energy that was the first thing that I fell in love with.

We spoke at the beach but we didn't exchange numbers.

We were both in relationships when we met.

Then there was a big summer festival at Dubrovnik where there were 20,000 people. The reason I went subconsciously was to bump into Andrea again.

I thought it would be unlikely, you couldn't even walk through the city there were so many people.

But the first bar I went into, I was ordering a drink, and I turned my head to the left and there was Andrea looking so handsome in his blue shirt, I remember it so vividly.

Vinko and Andrea communicated via email for three months until they could meet in person again. (Supplied)

2,743 emails between us

Vinko: After Croatia, Andrea and I continued this wonderful communication between us on email.

In three months, there were 2,743 emails between us.

I know the number because I photocopied them all to take to immigration months later when they asked, "Do you have proof of your relationship?"

So, Andrea and I had made a decision that we were going to meet again in person.

He had a wedding in Italy and I said, "Well, I'm coming to Bari, and you come and see me if you like, and we'll go from there."

Andrea had this whole romantic trip planned.

We stayed in medieval castles and villas, and it was a dream 10 days together.

And that was the end of our old lives, there was no going back.

Loading...

Andrea: In January 2011, I came to Australia to visit, and we went to see this woman at the immigration office and she really liked us.

We went there to investigate how we could do the next step in my relocating to Australia and she told us we could officially register our relationship.

So Vinko and I went from the immigration office to the births and marriages office, wearing swimsuits, sweating in 40-degree Sydney heat.

In comes this guy with bleached blonde hair who's never left Australia, and says, "I'm here to marry you." I couldn't understand a word of his accent.

Basically, we got "married" in the middle of the waiting room.

I left my medication where he could see it

Vinko: I had HIV (human immunodeficiency virus) for many years before meeting Andrea and was living a very kind of open life with it.

I spoke to two of my dearest friends about what was the right thing to do in telling Andrea and had written so many [unsent] letters to him.

But I made a call of not sharing it because I wanted to protect us. There was still so much stigma surrounding it.

It was a challenging time, but never during that time was Andrea ever in any threat or danger himself, because I was undetectable and always having checks. But the relationship was under threat because obviously there was dishonesty.

And eventually I knew it was going to come out, but then a day became a week, a week became a month, and a month became a year and then two years and then five years.

But I always believed in the power of love, and eventually I shared it by leaving my medication on the bench in the bathroom, and I knew it was going to be seen.

Vinko Anthony (right) and his partner Andrea Zaza use their own relationship as inspiration in their matchmaking agency. (Supplied: Sealey Brandt)

Andrea: Vinko always had some pills in the bathroom but on this day they'd changed.

So, I was like, "oh, strange" and I checked the box and they were antiviral pills for HIV.

And I went up and confronted him and said, "Is this true?"

But he was right to keep it from me because it would have been the end of us earlier in the relationship.

Then, I did my due diligence into really researching HIV and doing a test myself, and speaking with the doctor to find out exactly what does a diagnosis mean?

HIV in the 80s was always advertised as this scary thing.

This is the problem, you're stuck into that idea and that was how it was for me, until I really understood it.

Sign up to the ABC Lifestyle newsletter Get a mid-week boost and receive easy recipes, wellbeing ideas, and home and garden tips in your inbox every Wednesday. You’ll also receive a monthly newsletter of our best recipes.

From a love story to matchmaker

Vinko: Andrea and I had started a professional matchmaking service for gay men early on in our relationship, so there was a lot at stake.

When we sat together and talked about my diagnosis, he was so genuine and so sweet and so kind and said, "We are much bigger than this."

It was like a big weight off my shoulders. I felt safe.

Andrea: We had this feeling we could have done anything together.

It was the support of each other and the achievement of everything else, where it was empowerment, basically.

I never had that in my life [before].

Our love and our relationship are constantly growing. We evolve and develop together, respecting each other and supporting and acknowledging each other’s choices.

It's not always roses, but when you get older, you understand that the relationship gets better and better with time.

World.title: Women's group vows they're 'not going to get grey hair and do it quietly'
World.content:
To join any of the 370 Aussie Red Hatter chapters across Australia you must be a woman over 50 with a flair for dressing up, have an instinct for fun, and a royal name.

Anne Darling, aka Lady Darling Buds of May, is a founding member of South Wollongong's Ruby Ragers, an offshoot of the internationally renowned Red Hat Society.

The society started in the US in 1998 and quickly spread to more than 30 countries, as thousands of women across the globe celebrated a social club prioritising fun and friendship.

"We are a worldwide group of ladies, and it's purely a social group that connects, supports and encourages women in their pursuit of fun, friendship, freedom, fulfilment and fitness," Ms Darling said.

"When you're younger you compete with each other but that doesn't happen in this group.

"We're happy to share, discover and explore new interests constantly."

Aussie Red Hatters

The Queensland Girlfriends Giggle 2026 is the 16th convention for Aussie Red Hatters and the sixth one coordinated by Michelle Johnsson, aka Queen Desiderata from Brisbane Western Suburbs.

Women from the Aussie Red Hatters society performed the Hokey Pokey back in 2015, now they plan to do it again. (Supplied: Michelle Johnsson)

With 328 ladies registered from across Australia, the theme for October's event is fun and flowers, said Ms Johnsson, whose chapter is the wonderfully alliterative Magnificent Mesmerising M'Ladies.

Conventions organised by Ms Johnsson have taken place across the state, with this year's meet spotlighting Brisbane's Goodna Jacaranda Festival.

"On Friday we've got boats cruising to see the jacaranda trees in bloom, then on Saturday we're going to the Goodna Jacaranda Festival to do a flash mob dance to the hokey pokey," Ms Johnsson said.

" Little old ladies with grey hair, they get overlooked quite a bit, and that's the theme of the Red Hatters — that we're not going to get grey hair and do it quietly. "

Magnificent Mesmerising M’ladies and their Queen Desiderata at the Queensland Girlfriends Giggle, at Brisbane's Hilton Hotel in 2011. (Supplied: Michelle Johnsson)

The 75-year-old convenor said the goal was, as always, to "have a lot of fun".

"We've got an op-shop subgroup, a reading group, a coffee group and we've got really strong card players, and of course we've got a dance troupe who have been dancing for 18 years together now and we just have fun," she said.

"Two-thirds of my ladies are single, so it's their social life."

Women just want to have fun

The Ruby Ragers, a group of 50 ladies, held their first meeting in 2012 and a website, Aussie Hatting, lists nationwide chapters, events and notices.

"The Red Hat Society started in America in 1998 and the Australian group have the same name, but we aren't affiliated with them," Ms Darling said.

" We've just taken the idea and run with it, and it's been going in Australia probably 25 years. "

As this memento of the group depicts, members of the Aussie Red Hatters are a playful lot. (ABC Illawarra: Sarah Moss)

A poem written in 1961 by English poet Jenny Joseph, titled Warning, inspired the society.

"It was after the war years and she was tired of having to scrimp and save and she said when she got older she's going to do things she could never do, and would never have been allowed to do, like wear clothes that didn't match, hence the red hat and the purple clothes," Ms Darling said.

"An America woman saw the poem in England, thought it would be a good joke to send to her friend and bought her a red hat and a purple outfit."

And that is where it started, a simple poem reflecting on the theme of aging.

Loading...

The Ruby Ragers

Whilst being a member of the society requires one to have a royal name, having an alter ego also helps says Deborah Ricketts, Queen of South Wollongong's Ruby Ragers.

"I think wearing this outfit gives you the confidence to go beyond what you would normally do yourself," she said.

Deborah Ricketts, Wollongong's Ruby Ragers Queen Lunch-alot with her vice Red Hatter, Lady Laugh-a-lot. (ABC Illawarra; Sarah Moss)

"In my normal dress I wear plain jeans and T-shirts but come to Red Hats and I've got bling galore.

"It's purely a social group, we don't raise money or anything special other than have fun."

For the past 12 years, Irma Facey, Duchess of Bling Bling, has rummaged through opportunity shops for purple clothes and red hats to wear at the monthly outings.

"On my own I feel quite silly but with the whole group we just love it and we get so many comments, so many questions, people come up and say, 'Oh, you all look beautiful,'" she said.

"So, we're out there alright, it's just little girls dress-ups, but we're not little girls anymore," she said.

Aussie Red Hatter Marion Keating enjoys her monthly get-togethers with other members. (ABC Illawarra: Sarah Moss)

World.title: 'Outstanding' Tonga puts England on the brink of World Cup elimination
World.content:
Coach Kristian Woolf says Tonga showed off its new-found "depth and quality" in marching past England at the Rugby League World Cup.

The result left the English at risk of missing the semifinals for the first time.

With His Majesty King Tupou VI and Crown Prince Tupouto'a 'Ulukalala among the sellout 18,302 crowd in Perth on Saturday night, Tonga controlled the game when it counted, for a 30-12 win.

"We got more and more confident. What I liked the most was the way we defended; we put ourselves under pressure a couple of times, but our defence was outstanding," Woolf said after the game.

"You could see how much the game meant to us, and we showed that in our effort, and it's something that will carry us through the tournament."

The Mate Ma'a got better as the game went on, powering away from the world number three side to seal a victory which puts them in the box seat to reach the semifinals.

Kangaroos halfback's World Cup over Mitchell Moses will play no further part in Australia's Rugby League World Cup campaign after suffering a calf injury.

A first-half try to Stefano Utoikamanu set up a 10-0 lead at the break. But an early score from AJ Brimson was quickly countered, with two tries to Haumole Olakau'atu and one from Tolutau Koula asTonga ran away with the game.

A try to Dominic Young with under 20 minutes to go was only a consolation for England.

"We've done some special things with the Tonga team, but we're still quite new to beating tier-one nations, and England are that – they're a very strong team. We knew they would come out and be physical, and challenge us in different ways," Woolf said.

"It's a continuation of a journey that we're on. If you look at some of the young guys and some of the guys who are a little bit more experienced now, the experience they've got over the last three or four years has been outstanding.

"It's put us in a really good position. They're getting better and better. We've got depth and quality, and we can go and do something with it now."

Team Tonga took their bows to the big crowd in Perth after wrapping up a vital win over England. (Getty Images: Janelle St Pierre)

The defeat is a huge blow to England's chances.

England (or previously Great Britain) has never failed to reach the final four at a Rugby League World Cup.

This result leaves Brian McDermott's team likely to fall short, given the format of the competition.

The team was playing for the first time since losing to Australia in Leeds in November last year.

"It was a really good contest, and when it wasn't a contest, that was probably more to do with us in the errors that we made," McDermott said.

"They're a big team, strong team, and they've got some tremendous players in there. And I thought we we stuck toe-to-toe with them for nearly all the game."

England has to beat France on October 24 and Papua New Guinea on October 30 and hope other results and scores go their way, as they try to finish in the top two of the combined six-team Pool B and C.

Should England and Samoa end up with the same number of wins, the tiebreaker will be which nation has the better points-for-and-against differential.

With Samoa opening its campaign with a 78-4 smashing of France, it leaves England needing to post massive wins in its remaining two games to stay alive.

ABC/AAP

World.title: Basque migrants transformed town and left behind heritage handball court
World.content:
Most tourists don't even realise they visit Trebonne as they pass through the town en route to a famous north Queensland waterfall.

They drive through without stopping at the heritage-listed handball court that holds stories of workers who saved an industry and a culture that is experiencing a resurgence.

But Basque woman Marie-V Wherry has always delighted in telling people she is from the town just outside Ingham.

Marie-V Wherry grew up in Trebonne when the town was thriving with Basque migrants. (ABC News: James Tugwell)

"Trebonne was the centre of Basque civilisation in Australia, and I was always very proud to say that," she said.

"Then you'd have to explain who the Basques were."

The Basques are a European ethnic group from an area across France and Spain who have preserved their own language and culture.

Migrant 'saviours'

Three migrant recruitment drives, known as operations Emu, Eucalyptus and Kangaroo, brought at least 700 Basque workers to north Queensland in the 1950s to manually harvest sugar cane.

The Basque flag painted on the handball court in Trebonne. (ABC News: James Tugwell)

Historian and adjunct James Cook University lecturer Bianka Vidonja Balanzategui said the Basques, along with the Italians, were "saviours of the sugar industry" during the post-WWII labour shortages.

And they brought their culture with them.

A Basque man competing in a traditional weightlifting challenge, known as harrijasotze, in Ingham. (Supplied: Gloria Totoricaguena Egurrola, Australia Vasconia and the Lucky Country)

In 1959, a fronton or Basque handball court was built beside Trebonne pub to play pelota mano, a traditional game where competitors hit a ball against a wall and try to score points against their opponent.

Today, it's one of only two left in the country.

"This game is of particularly strong cultural importance," Dr Vidonja Balanzategui said.

"These men were young, active and fit and they brought with them their culture — their distinctive foods, their games. It was very important to them."

Centre of the community

Ms Wherry's parents were migrants and owned the bakery next to the pub and their house, where she still lives, was where people came knocking looking for a goat-skin ball to play with.

She remembers going to the town's butcher every day to get meat fat, which had been set aside for her, to rub on the ball to make it harder and fly faster.

Felix and José Maria Jayo (left) won the first ever game at the court against Juan Cruz Arriaga and Tomas Monasterio (right) in 1959. (Supplied: Bianka Vidonja Balanzategui)

And then, for a couple of shillings if she was lucky, she would watch the men play and score with chalk on the side of the concrete court.

In the evenings, her father would ice his hand, swollen from playing pelota mano, while his wife lectured him that he was too old to keep playing.

"Trebonne was humming in those days," Ms Wherry said.

The town had two grocers, a service station, two bakers, a sawmill, a post office, a pub, a butcher and its own petrol pump. But everything revolved around the handball court.

The two local schools held fairs on the court. It was a roller-skating rink and a skate park, and hosted dances and barbecues for the entire community.

Marie-V Wherry demonstrating how pelota mano was played on the fronton or handball court in Trebonne. (ABC News: James Tugwell)

"That was the gathering point: people coming to play pelota," Ms Wherry said.

The Basque canecutters from 200 kilometres south in Ayr would travel to Trebonne to play on the court and share news from their homeland.

Mechanisation and the end of an era

Dr Vidonja Balanzategui said Trebonne was a "home away from home" for the migrant workers.

Bianka Vidonja Balanzategui says Basque migrants always bring their culture with them. (ABC News: James Tugwell)

But the introduction of the mechanical harvester in the 1970s reduced the need for physical labourers and ended the Basque golden era in north Queensland. Most returned home.

The sound of the ball being hit against the wall has stopped. Local kids never learnt the rules for pelota mano.

The court cracked and became uneven and was eventually earmarked for demolition.

But it was saved by Hinchinbrook Shire Council, which acquired the site.

And in 2001 it was listed on the Queensland Heritage Register for its importance to the state's history and cultural heritage.

A mural of remembrance

In 2011, a mural was painted on the court depicting men playing pelota mano.

A mural was painted on the court in 2011 to make it look as if people were still playing pelota mano. (ABC News: James Tugwell)

"By putting the mural on it … our hope was that rather than tourists passing by on the way to Wallaman Falls, that they would actually stop, look and think for a moment: 'Oh look, there's people playing — oh no it's a mural' and might understand a little bit of the history of migration to our community and how important it was to both the economy and the cultural life of our district," Dr Vidonja Balanzategui said.

She said Trebonne was now "a shadow of its former self".

In May, Trebonne's pub called final drinks. The 430 locals were devastated.

They are left with only a nursing home, a state school and a mechanic.

A sign at the entry into Trebonne from Ingham in north Queensland. (ABC News: James Tugwell)

Yet Dr Vidonja Balanzategui said there was a renewed interest across Australia in Basque culture, food and language, especially in Sydney, which has the country's only other pelota mano court.

"Even though Trebonne might not offer all those facilities that it once had … Basque culture is not irrelevant today, even though the handball court, for instance, is no longer used," she said.

"The Basque community is vital … because it has young people that are interested."

A love for all things Basque

Occasionally in a cafe or shop, Ms Wherry will hear someone speaking Basque.

She cannot help but introduce herself and tell them about the Basque history in north Queensland and the handball court, her handball court, that was the centre of the Basque community.

"It's important that we do share that history and there is something that reminds us that Basque people were in Trebonne and Trebonne was important once," Ms Wherry said.

"We still are."

World.title: How to deal with spring weeds before they take over your garden
World.content:
Ah, spring!

As the southern hemisphere turns to face the sun, it is peak season for colourful wildflowers, exotic annuals and native shrubs.

Frustratingly for gardeners, it is also prime time for weeds.

Parkland in central Victoria infested with capeweed. (ABC News: Gavin McGrath)

Lawns, garden beds, and every nook and cranny with a patch of bare earth are relentlessly colonised and overrun by a familiar line-up of botanical pests.

Some are relatively benign for gardeners and more of an environmental problem.

Others, like the dreaded bindii or bindi-eye, are a literal pain.

Stepping on bindii weed is an experience one does not quickly forget. (Supplied: Harry Rose, iNaturalist Australia)

What weeds say about your soil

The adage suggests weeds offer a helpful insight into soil health.

ABC Local Radio gardening expert Rob Pelletier from Heritage Fruit Trees said that was only partly true.

"Certain weeds favour particular conditions, but they are not a reliable soil test and they are not necessarily 'repairing' the soil," Mr Pelletier said.

A better idea, he said, is to create the best possible growing conditions for the plants you want and avoid leaving bare soil for weeds to take hold.

Herbicides can control weeds, though many have side effects that make them less attractive for some gardeners.

ABC Local Radio gardening expert Rob Pelletier says different weeds need different treatments. (Supplied: Rob Pelletier)

Two non-chemical methods Mr Pelletier recommends involve sunlight, albeit in opposite ways.

Occultation involves covering weeds with an opaque object, such as a tarpaulin, to block the light they need to photosynthesise and grow. This is relatively gentle on soil biology.

Solarisation, on the other hand, uses sunlight and clear plastic to heat moist soil. This has an even greater effect on weeds, weed seed, pathogens and soil organisms, as it heats the soil and cooks the weeds.

Blackberry is a persistent perennial and a weed of national significance. (Supplied: Harry Rose, iNaturalist Australia)

Beyond the garden fence

While weeds can be a constant irritant for gardeners, they become an even greater problem when they escape the garden fence.

Gazania, introduced as a pretty ornamental flower from South Africa, shows how a species can become an environmental scourge.

Gazania is an invasive weed that was brought to Australia as an ornamental plant. (Supplied: Department of Environment and Water)

Environmental scientist Kate Blood, a former weeds management program manager with the Victorian government, says the damage they cause is immeasurable.

"In native grasslands and woodlands, gazanias crowd out indigenous plants that provide essential habitat for wildlife," she said.

"They are also becoming a serious problem for farmers, spreading into paddocks and cropping land."

Researchers are searching for practical, affordable and effective ways to manage them.

Horticulturist and weed expert Kate Blood says gazanias can have a serious impact on farmland. (Supplied: Kate Blood)

Ms Blood says weeds enter your garden or lawn in a variety of ways, but once they become weeds, little can be done.

"Ever had a random new plant like ivy or lantana pop up in your garden? Chances are its seeds were carried there in bird droppings or arrived through one of the many other ways plants spread — on the wind, in water, on clothing, animals or vehicles," she said.

"This is how invasive garden plants escape beyond the backyard, finding their way into bushland, waterways and native grasslands.

" What you plant in your garden can have a profound and lasting impact on nature around you, even if you live in a large town or city. "

Ms Blood is the Weed Society of Victoria president. Her advice to reduce the spread of weeds in the first place is:

Replace invasive garden plants with safer alternatives.

invasive garden plants with safer alternatives. Select garden plants carefully, checking their weed potential before buying or planting.

garden plants carefully, checking their weed potential before buying or planting. Dispose of garden waste responsibly to prevent invasive plants spreading beyond the garden fence.

"A beautiful garden shouldn't come at the expense of the natural environment around it," she said.

Colonisers, exploders, and persistent perennials

There is no one-size-fits-all solution for the multitude of invasive weeds that pop up during spring.

Many could be classified into three groups, said Mr Pelletier, each with a different control strategy required.

Meet the six Insect of the Year finalists Which of these six stunning critters will be the 2026 ABC Australian Insect of the Year? Vote now.

"You can look at colonisers which exploit bare or poor ground," he said.

"Then there are annual weeds that suddenly explode into growth and seed.

"And there are your persistent perennials, which keep coming back from underground parts."

Coloniser weeds: capeweed (Arctotheca calendula), scotch thistle (Onopordum acanthium), and dandelion (Taraxacum officinale). (Supplied: Zachary Rayne, Quentin Groom, Wouter Koch, iNaturalist Australia)

Colonisers

Colonisers are weeds that thrive where desirable plants are struggling, or the soil is bare.

Examples: Capeweed, dandelion, flat-weed, plantain, many thistles.

Control: Remove young plants, improve soil conditions, relieve compaction where needed, and keep soil covered with mulch, lawn or desirable plants.

Spring exploders: bittercress (Cardamine Hirsuta), chickweed (Stellaria media), and cleavers (Galium aparine). (Supplied: insiderelic, Erik Schiff, Harry Rose, iNaturalist Australia)

Spring exploders

These are weeds that often germinate through winter, then grow and seed rapidly during spring.

Examples: Chickweed, cleavers/sticky weed, fumitory, bittercress, sow thistle and annual grasses.



Control: Hoe or pull them while small and, most importantly, before they seed. Mulch afterwards.

Persistent perennials: blackberry (Rubus fruticosus), onion weed (Asphodelus fistulosus), and soursob (Oxalis pes-caprae). (Supplied: M. quinquenervia, insiderelic, Simon Tonge, iNaturalist Australia)

Persistent perennial weeds

These weeds survive through bulbs, rhizomes or deep roots, so simply removing the tops rarely works.

Examples: Soursob, onion weed, couch, bindweed and blackberry.

Control: Dig out the underground parts where practical, repeatedly remove regrowth, smother with an opaque tarp, solarise suitable areas, or use an appropriate systemic herbicide.

World.title: AI helps to track lobsters when 'no two shells are the same'
World.content:
After nearly three weeks at sea, Joe Sayers docks a boat filled to the brim with treasure — it's red, thorny and alive.

"There is one in here, I know there's 220 millimetres just in the carapace … there's a couple of fish in here that are probably going to be three, four kilos, I'd say, somewhere there," he said.

" A couple of monsters. "

Tasmania's southern rock lobster industry is bouncing back after some unsteady years. (ABC News: Bec Pridham)

Every year, Tasmania's commercial fishers catch just over 1,000 tonnes of southern rock lobster, valued at about $90 million.

While things are now on the up, it's been a tough few years for the industry, brought on by trade restrictions and a domestic market flooded with cheap lobsters.

Fisher Joe Sayers says the overheads of lobster fishing are only growing. (ABC News: Kate Nickels)

"Now we're up to getting a few dollars in the bank from better prices, but our costs are going up … all the time, like fuel and baits," Mr Sayers said.

" So, you outlay a lot of money before you go to sea, you can outlay say $50,000 before you even throw the lines off. "

But for Mr Sayers, it's a way of life, and after more than 30 years at sea, he wants to hand over an industry in good shape to the next generation.

Southern rock lobsters are caught measured, photographed and recorded as part of a new Lobster AI program, 01 September 2026 (ABC News: Bec Pridham)

'No two shells the same'

Scientists from the University of Tasmania's Institute for Marine and Antarctic Studies (IMAS), in partnership with Fiordland Lobster Company and the South Australian Lobster Company, are trying to ensure just that, through newly developed artificial intelligence (AI) technology.

Scientists Dean Giosio and Quinn Fitzgibbon photograph a lobster to see if it's in the database. (ABC News: Bec Pridham)

"It's just like a fingerprint or facial recognition technology," associate professor at IMAS Quinn Fitzgibbon said.

"We've used AI machine learning to look at the features on the shell of the lobster, and amazingly, we've been able to show that this technology can pick up those features and they're individual.

" There's no two shells the same. "

The AI technology has been developed by Dean Giosio, Quinn Fitzgibbon and Tara Kelly from the Institute for Marine and Antarctic Studies. (Supplied: Institute for Marine and Antarctic Studies)

It's as simple as a quick snap on an smartphone.

If the lobster has been photographed before, the AI recognises it, and if it hasn't, into the database it goes, joining thousands of others from across Australia and New Zealand.

"Now for the first time ever, to be able to trace a lobster from where it's captured … to where it might end up in a market or a restaurant in Sydney or China, it's actually a really big deal," Dr Fitzgibbon said.

This lobster has been scanned before. (ABC News: Bec Pridham)

The team has tested the AI under various scenarios, finding it recognises a lobster three years on, dressed up in barnacles and algae, or with a fresh exoskeleton.

It can even recognise it cooked.

In time, the idea is consumers themselves will be able to photograph their dinner and know exactly where it came from.

Southern rock lobsters are caught, measured, photographed and recorded. (ABC News: Bec Pridham)

Tackling distrust around product misplacement

The technology could be transformative for exporters like Michael Blake, who processes up to 300,000 lobsters per year at his Bicheno facility.

"It's the most premium-priced lobster in the world," he said.

" When you eat this lobster sashimi, there's nothing else like it in the world you can compare it to, and it really does stand alone. "

Exporter Michael Blake hopes the technology will help Tasmanian southern rock lobster reach new markets. (ABC News: Bec Pridham)

Scientists physically tag lobsters during population surveys, but that's not viable for the industry because tags can be removed or forged.

That means once fish leave the state, there's no way of proving where they came from, and money to be made from branding a foreign lobster as prized southern rock lobster.

Once lobsters are exported, they can end up in tanks with lobsters from Australia and other parts of the world. (ABC News: Bec Pridham)

"The lobsters are taken out of the boxes and placed in tanks with other lobsters from other countries, as well as from Australia," Mr Blake said.

" It's all mixed up and we have no idea if it's our lobsters, it's a New Zealand lobster, it's a South African lobster, the consumer really doesn't know. "

He is hopeful AI could help break into new markets, like the European Union, and strengthen trust in existing ones.

"Giving some of those restaurateurs overseas the confidence that this is guaranteed to come from here, will put the lobster on plates that it's currently not on," Mr Blake said.

Fresh off the boat, lobsters are weighed and graded for export. (ABC News: Bec Pridham)

Improving fisheries management

The scientists are now working to advance the technology for the processing sector, training it to record information like sex, size, colour and defects, and eventually, vitality.

"Most of these lobsters are exported overseas to China, that's a long trip, if the lobster's not healthy and vital, it unfortunately might not make that journey," Dr Fitzgibbon said.

Associate Professor Quinn Fitzgibbon hopes he and the team can further develop the technology for the processing sector and the fishery. (ABC News: Kate Nickels)

Down the track, the they also want to develop it for the fishery, so commercial and recreational fishers, and even citizen scientists, can contribute to the database.

Instead of piercing lobsters, the tags could become digital.

Scientists regularly conduct population surveys which inform decisions about the fishery. (ABC News: Bec Pridham)

IMAS usually has only one or two observers out at a time, but there are almost 100 commercial boats, presenting potential for much more data to inform management decisions.

Wild Fisheries Program leader John Keane says the AI could mean much more data. (ABC News: Bec Pridham)

"It may not necessarily change the catch limits, but it will give us more assurance that our recommendations to government are accurate and the catch is sustainable," IMAS senior research fellow John Keane said.

The Wild Fisheries Program leader said data would also be close to real-time, allowing quicker responses, which is useful given productivity declines brought on by climate change and habitat loss from the migration of the long-spined sea urchin.

Scientists hope the AI technology will ensure a profitable and sustainable future fro the southern rock lobster industry. (ABC News: Kate Nickels)

New horizons for southern rock lobsters

It's the kind of innovation that is making Mr Sayers optimistic about where things are headed.

"It's very good that at least people are interested and trying to do what's best for the industry, to look forward to the future of the industry," he said.

" It's came a long way over the years and it can probably go a long way again. "

World.title: Siblings with feet turned backwards get life-changing care
World.content:
Mum Lisa Kassau had never left her village on a tiny volcanic island in Vanuatu.

But that was before a life-changing opportunity allowed her to fly to Australia to help her children walk.

Siblings Anis, 13, and Melanie, 3, were both born with severe structural talipes, often called clubfoot.

The condition, which can run in families, had been uncorrected in the pair for so long that their feet were turned backwards.

It affects one in 1,000 babies born in Australia.

Mum Lisa Kassau with her daughter Melanie and son Anis on their last day in Canberra. (ABC News: Simon Beardsell)

Seven months of donated physiotherapy and surgeries in Canberra have allowed the pair to walk.

"I miss my family [but it's] important for my children to walk," Ms Kassau said.

"I live in my fields a long way away [and there's] no treatment," she said about the island of Tanna.

Ms Kassau now marvels at her children as they walk and play; the trio is thankful as they prepare to fly home.

"I can live now," she said.

Boy stares at new feet

Within 24 hours of arriving in Australia, senior physiotherapist with Canberra Health Services Melanie Ryan had applied stretching and put the children in plaster up to their thighs. That plaster was then changed once or twice a week.

"Melanie certainly engaged with us beautifully and would play games, but as soon as we'd go to put a plaster on, she well and truly got cross with us and told us off," Ms Ryan said about her three-year-old patient.

Canberra Health Services senior physiotherapist Melanie Ryan (right) and physiotherapist Dan Myyrylainen with the Kassau siblings. (Supplied)

" There were a couple of occasions where we thought she was being quite cheeky and saying some tough stuff to us. The mum refused to tell us what she was saying, her older brother also refused [but] he was very much chuckling. "

Ms Ryan worked with physiotherapist Dan Myyrylainen and Dr Blaise Wardle, who performed surgeries on the siblings.

She said a moment she would always remember was when Anis put his feet out in front of him and stared at them.

"I'd say to him, 'do they look different?' And he would just smile at me," Ms Ryan said.

"I think he'd gotten so used to his feet being turned for such a long time that I don't think he realised it was going to be possible for his feet to be corrected and to look like his friends'."

Physiotherapist Melanie Ryan treating the Kassau siblings. (Supplied)

"It's great to be able to use our skills for families who otherwise wouldn't have access to it," she said.

The care is possible under a memorandum of understanding between the ACT government and Rotary Oceania Medical Aid for Children (ROMAC) which brings sick babies and children to Canberra for critical care.

Goal to help 50 kids

Retired nurse and midwife Sandra Goldstraw has helped 33 Pacific Islander children through ROMAC. (ABC News: Nick Haggarty)

The Kassau family was welcomed into Sandra Goldstraw's Canberra home.

The Rotarian, who was instrumental in establishing ROMAC's Canberra operation, is a retired nurse and midwife who has housed, fed and clothed 33 Pacific Islander children, including Anis and Melanie.

"And there are more children out there who need our help, who are just like our children," Ms Goldstraw said.

" They are loved just like our mums love us. "

Three-year-old Melanie Kassau can walk after receiving care for talipes. (ABC News: Simon Beardsell)

Ms Goldstraw hopes to help 50 children.

And next week she will host a baby and mother, also from Vanuatu, when the three-month-old boy who has a lung condition is discharged from a special care nursery in Canberra.

The Kassau family spent seven months in the ACT so the children could recieve life-changing care. (ABC News: Simon Beardsell)

Quiet duo thrives

Ms Goldstraw said when the Kassau siblings arrived they were very quiet before developing interests in their new surroundings.

"They started to really like TV because they've never had the TV at home, and we have an extra phone, so they kept on playing games on the phone.

" And Melanie, well, she's just a sweet little three-year-old who was quite noisy at times, and she loved to dance around. "

Thirteen-year-old Anis Kassau was supported at Gold Creek High School. (ABC News: Simon Beardsell)

When older brother Anis was not in hospital, he was supported to attend Gold Creek High School for two terms.

"They looked after him so well. They even had a special teacher to guide him," Ms Goldstraw said.

And although there were significant language barriers, she said she had a wonderful connection with the children's mother.

"She'd always like to have a hug," she said about Ms Kassau.

"I could see that she was so happy to see her children progressing with their treatment; she would smile when she saw them walking around and having a bit of fun at the physio department," she said.

ROMAC started 20 years ago and has helped about 600 children, while the Canberra operation began in 2010 with capacity to help four children each year.

World.title: Forget Starbucks – welcome to the birthplace of China’s coffee industry
World.content:
WorldAsiaInside China Forget Starbucks – welcome to the birthplace of China’s coffee industry Lisa Visentin October 18, 2026 — 9:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Yunnan, China: On a remote mountain slope in south-west China, bamboo trays of freshly picked red coffee cherries are drying in courtyards and on the rooftops of farmers’ homes in the tiny village of Zhukula. Much of the fruit has been harvested from trees planted next to an old church more than a century ago by French missionaries who brought Arabica saplings, along with Catholicism, across the border from Vietnam. The village’s nascent Christian conversion didn’t survive the religious purges of the Cultural Revolution, but the coffee trees are now recognised as the oldest in the country, making Zhukula the birthplace of China’s coffee cultivation. Coffee roasting practices have remained unchanged in the village for decades, with the beans toasted over high heat using a wood-fired oil drum and cast-iron work for more than an hour. In this corner of China, long days ploughing and harvesting the mountainside are book-ended by coffee, not tea.



“Ever since I was little, as far back as I can remember, there have been coffee trees growing all around here,” says Li Jinrong, 57, a third-generation coffee farmer. “We make coffee as soon as we get up in the morning, drink it, go out to work and then have another cup before dinner.” Li Jinrong’s wife removes freshly roasted coffee beans from the hot cast-iron wok. The village of Zhukula has just one road in and out for its 83 households, reachable only by driving for hours along slender hairpin bends that snake around a mountain range. Li invites us into his farmhouse after we poke our heads through an open doorway leading to his courtyard, drawn in by a striking mound of yellow corn cobs baking in the sun and a noisy cat.



His home is a modest three-storey brick structure, centred around an open-air communal room with a concrete-slab floor. One corner functions as a kitchen, with a rice cooker and a camping stove rigged up to a single power board looped around a nail in the wall, while a collection of mismatched plastic stools surrounds a basic dining table. In the courtyard, he empties a rice sack filled with green coffee beans – shelled from their cherry skins – into a wood-fired roasting pit, fashioned out of an oil drum and large cast-iron work. Loading With a cooking shovel, he continuously turns the beans, a process that takes more than an hour to achieve a deep roast. It might seem nostalgically authentic, but it’s a laborious task that modern coffee manufacturers long ago outsourced to roasting machines. While China’s surging taste for coffee helped drive global prices to record highs in 2025, few, if any, farmers in Zhukula have grown rich from coffee.



“We grow coffee beans to make a living, but coffee alone isn’t enough. The problem is that we don’t have much farmland here,” Li says. “Coffee consumption [in China] has increased, but our area is small, so sales are unstable.” A woman in Zhukula sorts freshly harvested coffee cherries in a woven bamboo tray. Until about a decade ago, Yunnan was more famous for its tea production. Today, the sprawling mountainous region produces almost all of China’s coffee beans, an industry that has boomed as cafe culture has exploded across the country. China still trails miles behind Europe and the United States in terms of global coffee consumption, accounting for just 3 per cent, but it’s the fast-growing market, rising 150 per cent over the past decade.



It’s big business, with large commercial farms harvesting thousands of tonnes of coffee beans each year. You can find Yunnan beans in speciality coffee shops around the world, Australia included. But today, most of the region’s produce is consumed domestically, fuelled by the rapid expansion of coffee chains such as Chinese giant Luckin Coffee, which has opened 30,000 stores across the mainland since its first in Beijing in 2017. Boutique cafes serving oat milk lattes, iced Americanos and various berry infused, caramel-lashed, pistachio-rimmed concoctions are now abundant across Shanghai, Beijing and other major cities. This growing demand has helped pull farmers out of poverty in rural Yunnan, which remains one of China’s poorest provinces. The industry’s rise is also a case study in China’s 1980s pivot from a wholly planned economy to state-supported private enterprise and land cultivation, while also highlighting how rural land reform continues to constrain small-scale farmers.



Which boats have been lifted highest by this rising tide has depended heavily on geographical luck and the Communist Party’s “visible hand” in picking industrial and agricultural winners. Capitalism with Chinese characteristics Gao Jianyun, 63, chairman of Gaosheng Coffee, a company he built from his family’s farm in Baoshan in China’s Yunnan province. About half a day’s drive from Zhukula, towards China’s border with Myanmar, the sweeping valleys of Baoshan are blanketed in coffee trees, popping with red fruit. Many of them are owned by private commercial farms such as Gaosheng Coffee Manor, a family operated estate that runs a cafe, cupping room and tasting courses, while its German-imported industrial roasters churn through thousands of kilograms of beans each week.



Once an export-oriented business that used to count Nestlé and Starbucks as its largest clients, Gaosheng is now almost entirely focused on China’s domestic market. Related Article Inside China The Beijing pigeons that circle Mao before flying home “Luckin Coffee, Cotti Coffee and Mixue are our biggest customers. They’re our gods,” Gaosheng Coffee chairman Gao Jianyun says. The company is one of several large coffee enterprises that have sprung up in Baoshan over the past two decades. Its roots trace back to a 1950s state policy designating the region as one of China’s agricultural engine rooms, where farmers were instructed to grow coffee. “At that time, planting coffee wasn’t something they wanted to do themselves. It was mandated by the state’s planned economy,” says Gao, whose parents were among the first coffee farmers in the area.



Similar to the Li family in Zhukula, the Gao family also has three generations rooted in coffee farming, but their trajectories couldn’t be starker. As China’s economy opened up, and the government poured resources into making Baoshan a coffee cultivation powerhouse, the Gaos scaled up and invested in modern equipment, whereas the Zhukula farmers today remain limited by isolation, difficult terrain and low-earning capacity. When Gao joined his parents working on their farm in the early 1980s, all fresh coffee cherries were still purchased centrally by the collective, and his role was to calculate and distribute wages based on farmers’ planting area. Workers sort through green coffee beans, removing the flawed ones, at Gaosheng Coffee in Yunnan province, China. Luorui Xiang By 2005, the family had set up its own company, which today owns 34 hectares of coffee plants in Boashan and 80 hectares in the nearby Pu’er region and employs 100 people. Under China’s rural land system, farmers cannot buy or sell farmland, but they can lease their land-use rights to others, enabling wealthier operators and co-operatives to turn fragmented plots into larger estates. Gao says these farmers’ incomes have increased several times over. Meanwhile, Gaosheng Coffee is on track to make 120 million yuan ($26 million) this year through sales of green beans and packaged coffee products.



In the company’s boardroom, an airbrushed portrait of Chinese President Xi Jinping hangs on the wall, mounted alongside various golden plaques and accolades the business has been awarded. It’s a nod to the link between private commercial success and state support – particularly in the agriculture sector – under China’s model of “socialism with Chinese characteristics”. “We are also actively working with the government to expand our operations and increase production capacity,” Gao says. His daughter, Gao Jie, who studied a master of business administration in New York and now heads the company’s brand strategy, is aiming for a 20 per cent increase in sales this year. Some villagers in Zhukula keep small numbers of livestock in pens next to their farmhouses. Coffee farming frozen in time Back in Zhukula, the remote, rugged beauty of the mountain is also the farmers’ curse – a paradox familiar across rural China. Li’s house is the last at the end of the village, where the road abruptly gives way to a sheer drop to the valley and the Yupao River that flows through it.



The path to Li’s house is too narrow for cars and too steep for bicycles. It winds past his neighbours’ homes, where a few pigs, goats, cows and chickens are kept in cramped wooden pens next to their living quarters. It’s a portrait of communist agrarianism frozen in time, with faded Communist Party slogans painted in red on the outside of homes, urging villagers to march together towards prosperity. “Contentment with poverty is shameful. Overcoming poverty is honourable,” one slogan reads. A goat pokes its head through a window in a farmhouse stable in Zhukula village. A Communist Party slogan painted on the wall warns about “dark and evil forces”, a reference to organised crime. Luorui Xiang There’s a party activities centre in the village, while a few houses fly the hammer and sickle flag out front, identifying local members with leadership roles in the community. It’s indicative of how party governance is woven into the fabric of even China’s smallest villages. In the 1980s, after China abandoned the Mao-era commune and collective farming system, Li’s family was assigned 36 coffee trees under a policy that allocated land based on family size. Since then, it has expanded its coffee crop while also farming walnuts, Sichuan pepper and corn, but scaling up remains impossible on a plot of less than a hectare.



Higher bean prices have boosted the family’s income, but it’s still in the realm of subsistence rather than wealth generation. In a good year, Li and his 34-year-old son, Jiangfu – who also lives in the village with his wife and young daughter – harvest just under 1000 kilograms of coffee cherries. A Zhukula villager with fresh coffee cherries. The crop is the main source of each household’s annual income of about 25,000 yuan ($5400) – in line with the national average for rural farmers, but less than half what a migrant worker can earn as a delivery driver in Beijing or Shanghai. “Sales have gradually improved. In the past, many people didn’t know about our coffee, and it was difficult to sell,” Jiangfu says.



Now there’s a reliable stream of coffee shop owners, tourists and farmers’ friends and relatives who buy their beans, with demand outpacing their supplies, he says. Related Article China relations ‘Work is getting harder and harder to find’: On the street with China’s gig workers The village has clearly benefited from government efforts to transform it into a tourist destination, with newly paved roads, community toilet facilities and the church converted into a museum that chronicles Zhukula’s legacy as China’s first coffee village. A number of Li’s neighbours are building new homes and Li himself has partially renovated his house, with the support of government subsidies. Still, it is a world away from where some of Zhukula’s beans end up, served in trendy urban cafes as flat whites or experimental signature drinks for $10 a cup, alongside tasting notes exhorting the rich, nutty flavour of Yunnan coffee. World.title: How this relentless Australian bowling attack stacks up against the greats
World.content:
SportCricketAustralian cricket How this relentless Australian bowling attack stacks up against the greats Greg Chappell October 18, 2026 — 9:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Australia’s Test bowling attack ranks among the best in the world over the last 50 years, having broken new ground as a quartet and taking an unprecedented number of wickets as a four-man unit. Statistically, Pat Cummins, Mitchell Starc, Josh Hazlewood and Nathan Lyon sit comfortably in the same pantheon as some of the best West Indian attacks from the late ’70s. Loading Michael Holding, Andy Roberts, Joel Garner, Malcolm Marshall and Colin Croft combined hostility with control. People have described facing them as like facing an execution squad, offering no respite from either end. In Durban against South Africa last week, Australia out-bowled, out-batted and out-fielded their opponents and deserved their decisive victory. Central to the win was the attack.



Like past combinations from the late 1990s and early 2000s – comprising Glenn McGrath, Shane Warne, Jason Gillespie and Brett Lee – today’s attack offers the ultimate balance of precision, elite spin, pace and nagging persistence. The South African quartet of Dale Steyn, Morne Morkel, Vernon Philander, and Jacques Kallis from the late 2000s and mid-2010s also dominated an era favouring batting. Australian batsman Bruce Laird is struck on the hand by a Michael Holding delivery in 1980. Fairfax Media Then there was Pakistan’s outstanding attack: Imran Khan, Wasim Akram and Waqar Younis, with the spin of Abdul Qadir, another brilliant group who turned the old ball into lethal weapons capable of tearing through middle orders. Like the great West Indian combinations of the late 20th century and the Australian attack of the early 2000s, Cummins’ men thrive on discipline.



Hazlewood mirrors McGrath’s relentless probing line; Cummins attacks the stumps with fuller lengths; Starc provides the left-arm angle, swing, and X-factor pace; Lyon provides the control and sustained pressure of an elite spinner. While the historic West Indian pace battery holds the crown for sheer terror, and the 2000s Australian attack for ultimate match-winning balance, this crop matches them in longevity, relentless line and length and the ability to consistently grind down opponents through partnership bowling. In Kingsmead, batsman Matt Renshaw set the tone for Australia in the first innings with support from Cummins and Lyon. The desperation to post as high a score as possible from 6-124 on a challenging wicket was obvious. On his return to Test cricket, Nic Maddinson looked so desperate not to get out in the first innings that he made scoring look impossible. He soaked up much of the strike, and his dismissal was almost a relief to him.



Marnus Labuschagne looked more intent on scoring, and his resulting footwork was crisper. We may yet see the real Labuschagne by the end of the series. The real Steve Smith, meanwhile, is never far away. His dismissal soon after lunch on the first day, though, surprised everyone. South Africa didn’t bowl badly, but they didn’t bowl enough good balls in clumps to put pressure on the middle order on a wicket that was offering bounce. South Africa’s spinners were disappointing. They didn’t bowl a line or length suited to the conditions, so the Australians scored easily. Josh Hazlewood and skipper Pat Cummins form half of the most fearsome bowling quartet in Test cricket today. AP Photo/Themba Hadebe Renshaw was a tremendous success in the middle order. His game against spin worked in the conditions. This part of his game has developed in recent years. With his sweeping, he is ambidextrous and drove the spinners to distraction by carefully choosing his shots. He doesn’t try to over-hit his sweeps, relying on timing and placement to taunt the bowlers. He is a big man and uses his reach to advantage. Cummins could easily have been a genuine all-rounder if his bowling hadn’t demanded so much. He has a solid defence and an abundance of power. He was determined to lead by example, and his partnership with Renshaw was critical to the match.



Lyon is a fierce competitor who has become a better-than-useful tail-ender, handling short balls with the aplomb of a higher-rated batter. He is the perfect foil for a batter in this situation. His defence is solid; he is fearless and rotates the strike well. The Australians again gave a masterclass in bowling in any conditions through immaculate lines and lengths. Few have matched their ability to bowl together for extended periods. It must be like water torture to bat against them. Cummins is a class act. His return from injury to bowl at an elite pace, full and at the stumps, is exceptional. He consistently directs his bouncer with precision and utilises it efficiently, seldom wasting it. His default length is fuller than most, so every ball demands a response, and his full-blooded attack demands wickets. He is inspiring. Starc looked a little rusty, but that is the beauty of this group. If one doesn’t get you, someone else will. Hazlewood was brilliant. His line rarely changes, and he bowls a suffocating length. It must feel as if you are batting against a boa constrictor. It is only a matter of how long it takes for him to squeeze the life out of you.



Hazlewood and Lyon have returned from serious injuries and have resumed business as usual. Their professionalism showed in how wholeheartedly they committed to their rehabilitation. Related Article Australian cricket Reversal of fortune: Hazlewood says old-ball swing ‘crucial’ to South Africa triumph Lyon showed his opposition spinners how to bowl in the conditions. His line, length, and pace were ideal, and his relentlessness was top-class. The opposition spinners gave the Australians too much room, which let the pressure off too often. Lyon’s pace, with maximum revs and line, is much harder to reverse-sweep than his two opposition spinners. The second-innings situation gave Maddinson some freedom, and he looked like a different player. Had he been more fortunate with the timing of his earlier selection, he could easily have played much more Test cricket.



Australia got some luck in this Test because South Africa were without their two best pace bowlers, Kagiso Rabada and Lungi Ngidi. Had Rabada played, the outcome could have been very different. His absence was deeply felt, and the Proteas will need him for the rest of the series to change the result. With Steve Smith passing the concussion tests, he will play in the second Test. That is a bonus for Australia, as he remains the group’s most reliable batter. His batting is key for Australia, and so is his brilliant fielding. Australia would not want to lose him. The bowling attack and Steve Smith are still critical to the side’s success.

World.title: King Dobby ate a Croc and a bottle top – leaving his owners an impossible $6000 choice
World.content:
NationalVictoriaPets King Dobby ate a Croc and a bottle top – leaving his owners an impossible $6000 choice James Costa October 18, 2026 — 8:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month.
