“King” Dobby, as the Chihuahua Dachshund cross is called, wasn’t behaving like his normal, energy-filled and demanding self. He wasn’t playing, he was lethargic, and sat shaking on the corner of the bed – usually he’s plonked right in the middle of his owners. His family knew something was wrong and rushed him to the Lort Smith Animal Hospital. Dobby, the Chihuahua Dachshund cross, had to be rushed to the animal hospital after eating a Croc and bottletop. Ruby Alexander Turns out he had eaten an olive oil bottle top and chewed up a Croc sandal. The emergency surgery, necessary for the life-threatening blockage, was set to cost them almost $6000. The Aarons family – Caitlin, Jai and their two sons – were distraught. They couldn’t afford the massive vet bill and had to stop and contemplate letting Dobby go.



“[I was] feeling lower than crap because, like, I can’t afford to get my fur baby fixed,” said Caitlin. How on earth, she thought, would she tell her kids their dog wouldn’t be coming home? The Aarons are not alone. Across Victoria, families are skipping vet visits, missing out on preventative care and, increasingly, facing the difficult decision of either incurring debt or euthanising their pet. A 2025 survey by Animal Medicines Australia, the peak body representing the animal health industry, found that about 16 per cent of pet owners had accessed financial assistance to cover the cost of veterinary care, and that one in six people skipped taking their dog or cat to the vet to save money. Last year, 54 per cent of all people who visited pet hospital Lort Smith were struggling financially and received discounted care from the not-for-profit.



“Financially, it was incredibly stressful,” Caitlin said. “It was the day before payday, we don’t have pet insurance, and we couldn’t use Afterpay. I had to borrow money from family just to get started. I was panicking, wondering what we were going to do and calling everyone for help.” Caitlin, Jai, Laurence and James Aarons with their dog, Dobby. Ruby Alexander After much stress, Dobby got the surgery he needed. Lort Smith has a fund for people experiencing financial hardship. That fund, said Caitlin, covered almost $4000 for the surgery, with the family borrowing the remaining $2000 with a no-interest loan from Good Shepherd. “I was so worried about paying for treatment that I couldn’t even food shop,” Caitlin said. “We were just eating whatever was left in the fridge, hoping for the best but preparing for the worst.” Lort Smith chief executive Frances Mirabelli said the hospital is eating into its cash reserves to keep pace with rising costs and surging demand for its care.



To manage the volume, Mirabelli has rostered extra vets, staff and volunteers. But the model relies heavily on full-paying clients to subsidise care for those who cannot afford it – a balance that is becoming harder to maintain as household budgets tighten across the state. With a state election approaching, the hospital is calling on both the government and the opposition to commit $1 million in targeted funding. “That’d help us help thousands of animals, and have a massive impact on so many people,” Mirabelli said. Lort Smith Animal Hospital chief executive Frances Mirabelli. Simon Schluter “It’s the emergencies that are the problem,” Mirabelli said, “that’s when it starts get really expensive. That’s not because we’re making huge profits – it’s just because that’s the cost of care at the moment.” Beyond that emergency relief, Lort Smith is also seeking an additional $4 million commitment to expand its crisis relief animal boarding network for the pets of people experiencing family violence.

World.title: The leap second has been cancelled. It’s about time
World.content:
WorldEuropeDaylight saving The leap second has been cancelled. It’s about time K.R. Callaway October 18, 2026 — 8:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Every few years since 1972, computers, financial institutions, communications networks and other systems have had to reset their clocks by a single second. On Thursday, the international authority on timekeeping voted to abolish this contentious quirk of global synchronisation. The change will take effect in 2027. In a meeting of officials from the International Bureau of Weights and Measures, or BIPM, in France, the group axed the leap second, which had been established to align our clocks with Earth’s rotation. The practice was similar to that of the leap year, when an extra day is added to our calendars to keep us in sync with Earth’s orbit around the sun. Leap years are predictable, happening every four years. But leap seconds account for seemingly random irregularities in how fast Earth rotates, which has been causing trouble for timekeepers, including the looming possibility of needing a “negative leap second” because Earth’s spin is getting faster. Michael Wouters from the CSIRO with Australia’s atomic clock. Ben Rushton “This decision has become particularly timely because recent changes in the Earth’s rotation have raised the possibility of a first-ever negative leap second, which has never been experienced and that could create additional risks for critical infrastructures,” Noel Dimarcq, president of the BIPM’s committee for time and frequency, said in a statement.



In lieu of the added second, humankind will wait until an entire hour is needed to bring us back into synchronisation with the planet’s spin. This new practice is “just easier” to keep track of, said Patrizia Tavella, director of the bureau’s time department. Related Article Explainer

Daylight saving It’s daylight saving time again – but why do we have it at all? It’s unclear when this extra hour may be needed, but it might not happen for centuries. “It’s really just taking the problem well, well into the future,” said Andrew Novick, an electrical engineer and manager of the time and frequency division at the National Institute of Standards and Technology, or NIST, in Maryland. “It could be thousands of years before this leap hour happens.” For much of history, “the Earth was the best available clock”, Duncan Agnew, a geophysicist at Scripps Institution of Oceanography in California, explained during the meeting. Keeping time mostly involved ways of dividing how long it takes Earth to complete one rotation on its axis: Earth rotates at about 1000 mp/h (1600 km/h) on average, so a day equals 86,400 seconds.



By the mid-20th century, humans needed more timekeeping precision to support the advent of computers, international communications systems and space exploration. Enter atomic clocks, which measure time by tracking the tiny changes atoms undergo at regular intervals. These ultra-precise clocks ushered in a global way of keeping time: Coordinated Universal Time, or UTC, which was adopted in 1963. “You only know how good your clock is when you get a better clock,” Novick said. Sometimes gravitational interactions with other celestial bodies or the movements of air, water and rock on our dynamic planet can affect its rotation speed. Once clocks became more precise, these subtle shifts in Earth’s rotation became more noticeable, which is why we adopted the leap second. In recent decades, though, the added second posed two main problems for our digital systems. For starters, it can be a hassle to change the time by a single second and could even cause time-linked systems to temporarily shut down. Some tech giants such as Google adopted a “leap smear” instead, temporarily slowing down their clocks rather than adding the leap. What’s more, Earth’s rotation isn’t always lagging behind. The same forces that slow it down can also work in reverse, meaning that one day we might have a negative leap second. And while most of the digital systems that rely on UTC are prepared to jump ahead, far fewer have the code built in to handle a move backward in time.



The Earth has rotated on its axis at roughly 15 degrees an hour for about 4.6 billion years. Time zones, on the other hand, are an extremely recent human creation. Adobe Stock Since the 2000s, Earth’s rotation has been speeding up, driven by a combination of changes to Earth’s core and surface phenomena like the melting polar ice caps. This makes the need for a negative leap second more likely, and, in part, drove timekeepers to their decision to end the leap second. Related Article Explainer

Science Why do we have leap years (and what does Cleopatra have to do with them)? The vote was not unanimous. Delegates from Russia, whose satellites often have a built-in system for handling leap seconds, voted against the measure, and those from Belarus abstained. The differential between our clocks and Earth’s rotation is currently hovering around zero, meaning the next leap second could have easily been a negative one, Novick said. Still, Novick and other scientists said they will miss this little idiosyncrasy in the way we keep time.



“It’s the one time you could almost assure that NIST would be on the news,” Novick said, “because it gets people thinking about the Earth’s rotation, and about time.” This article originally appeared in The New York Times. Police have charged a teenager over multiple sexual offences allegedly committed against women on walking trails in Sydney’s northern beaches. “Following a public appeal, a 13-year-old boy was arrested after attending Mona Vale police station about 7.30pm,” NSW Police said in a statement on Saturday. Several women have reported sexual touching and harassment on the Narrabeen Lagoon trail over the past week. Internet He was charged overnight with three counts of behaving in an offensive manner near a public place and eight counts of sexually touching another person without consent. Police will allege that there were 11 separate incidents involving women and girls aged between 13 and 54 in the Narrabeen area, mostly between October 1 and 12.



Related Article Crime Multiple women allegedly targeted on northern beaches walking trails There was also an earlier incident, where a woman was allegedly spoken to inappropriately at the intersection of Waroon Road and Carawa Road, Cromer, about 6.45pm on September 7. Investigations began after three alleged incidents in two days, during which “a male allegedly approached women on walking trails, sexually touched them and then rode away on an e-bike”, police said. “In one of the incidents, the man also [allegedly] made inappropriate sexual comments.” Another woman came forward alleging that at the start of the month, she was sexually touched by a man at Narrabeen Lagoon and that he then rode away on an e-bike.



Two women further reported they had been sexually touched by a male riding an e-bike on October 12 as they walked along the lagoon near Bilarong Reserve. The teenager has been granted conditional bail to appear in a children’s court on November 4. Anyone with information, mobile phone or dashcam footage, or who may have witnessed any of the incidents is urged to contact Crime Stoppers on 1800 333 000. World.title: ‘Planned operation’: The test result that reveals a dangerous Trump betrayal
World.content:
Analysis WorldEuropeRussia-Ukraine war ‘Planned operation’: The test result that reveals a dangerous Trump betrayal David Crowe October 18, 2026 — 5:55am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. London: A satellite speed test on a European motorway is an unusual way to check whether Donald Trump can be trusted. But the test results are impossible to ignore when they challenge everything the American president claims about the war in Ukraine. The results also have implications for every American ally when the findings suggest the Trump administration has slowed the speed of the Starlink satellite network, and its Starshield military system, so Ukrainian targets are more exposed to Russian attacks. Donald Trump and Elon Musk pictured outside the White House in August. AP Just think of the gravity of that decision. All the signs suggest the Americans made a technical change that increased civilian casualties. Without Starlink working properly, Ukrainian drones lost the power to intercept Russian drones. The rational conclusion is that civilians died from a decision in Washington DC to limit the use of an American network.



The speed test was undertaken in recent days by Ukrainian personnel who took Starlink equipment into a nearby European Union country to check whether they would get the same slow speeds they experienced when using the terminals in Ukraine. Related Article Russia-Ukraine war Musk approached Trump to slow down Starlink in Ukraine The result? Starlink worked for vehicles travelling at 180km/h in Europe. In Ukraine, however, service was cut out for drones travelling at more than 161km/h. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky revealed the results to journalists on Saturday (Sunday AEDT) and explained why they mattered. When Ukrainian forces send a drone to intercept a Russian attack, he said, they “lose the drone” when it travels at a speed higher than the Starlink cap. While they could slow the drone, of course, that would only make it harder to intercept a Russian kamikaze drone heading for an apartment building.



Zelensky concluded that the technical limit on Starlink in Ukraine was no accident. “Limitations are in effect on the territory of Ukraine, and limitations are not in effect on the territory of the EU countries,” he said. “That is, this is a planned operation.” So, who planned it? This is a question every American ally, including Australia, should want answered. Trump denies being responsible and also tries to protect Elon Musk, the founder and controller of Starlink and its parent company, SpaceX. “It wasn’t me and I don’t think it was Elon,” he said on Friday.



Well, somebody in the Trump administration did it. The Telegraph reported on Friday that Musk suggested the move to Trump, who liked the idea. Reuters reported the order came from inside the White House. Trump claims he wants peace in Ukraine, but his latest decisions have the effect of helping Russia wage war. He has blocked funding for Ukraine, limited its access to Patriot interceptors, hedged on a security guarantee in any ceasefire and suggested Zelensky should cede more territory to Putin. He is also unwinding sanctions against Russia, starting with a deal to let the Kremlin make more money from diesel fuel exports. Loading “It’s immoral and it makes no sense,” the former US ambassador to Russia, Michael McFaul, said of the diesel and sanctions moves on US television. “What American national interest is advanced by these decisions? There’s none.” Australians should be watching this closely. Remember, it was only 18 months ago that Trump talked of having a way to limit the features of jet fighters used by allies. This “kill switch” talk alarmed the US defence industry, which feared it would lose sales.



Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney is responding carefully to what Trump says. He has started a review of a Canadian plan to buy a fleet of F-35 stealth fighters from the US. Canada has also gained “observer” status on a sixth-generation fighter being developed by the UK, Italy and Japan. Related Article Updated

Russia-Ukraine war ‘Betrayed’: Ukraine leader denounces Trump for siding with Russia amid row with Musk At a time when Australia is committed to buying US submarines under the AUKUS program, it is essential to confront the inherent risk in relying on the US under Trump. It is no longer science fiction to think that someone in Washington DC might want to “switch off” the military capability of an ally. Ukraine is not a formal US ally. Until Trump, however, it was promised full support from America under security agreements. Former president Joe Biden hedged on shipping some of the armaments Zelensky wanted, but he kept funding Ukraine to try to stop Russia because this was seen as vital to the interest of the US and its NATO allies. Yes, the head-spinning shift under Trump betrays Ukraine. But it does more than this. It warns all American partners of the danger of depending on an unreliable ally.



European leaders, like those in Australia, are extremely wary of offending Trump by directly criticising his decisions to help Putin. Their approach is to use optics, like the social media clips of their warm meetings with Zelensky, to show where they stand. Zelensky has a very different objective. He has acted to maximise attention on the American decision on Starlink speeds. The effect is to highlight the questions about Trump’s judgment, even if Zelensky risks an even greater rupture in his relationship with the president. What else can Zelensky do? There seems to be no benefit to Ukraine in staying quiet, so Zelensky seeks to make sure that Americans know what Trump has done. World.title: What my pilgrimage to Mecca taught me
World.content:
LifestyleLife & relationshipsReligion Opinion What my pilgrimage to Mecca taught me

Essan Dileri October 18, 2026 — 5:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

While on the journey to perform Hajj, the Muslim pilgrimage to Makkah (Mecca), I realised that Hajj was asking something much deeper of me. It was asking me to leave behind not only my home and possessions, but also my pride, attachments, fears and illusions of control. Essan Dileri in front of the Kaaba, in Mecca, as he does his hajj. Photo: Supplied When I entered ihram — the sacred state pilgrims enter, symbolised by simple clothing — I felt that something within me was being stripped away. The distinctions by which I sometimes measure myself seemed to lose meaning. I noticed that my nationality, education, appearance and social position became insignificant. I found myself standing before Allah (God) dressed simply, vulnerable and equal. The simplicity of ihram also made me think about the transience of this life. When I first saw the Kaaba, the sacred structure at the heart of the Grand Mosque in Makkah towards which Muslims around the world pray, I struggled to put my emotions into words. I had spent my life turning towards it in prayer, but suddenly I was standing before it. For a moment, the distance between what I had known intellectually and what I was experiencing spiritually disappeared. I felt small and humbled. I couldn’t stop crying. During Tawaf, the ritual of walking seven times around the Kaaba, I began to reflect on what occupies the centre of my life. I was physically circling the House of Allah, but inwardly I was asking myself: What does my heart revolve around? Is it Allah, or is it success, comfort, fear or the judgement of others?



That question stayed with me. Tawaf taught me that faith is not simply about where I turn my body during prayer. It is about where I turn my heart when I am scared and where I place my hopes when I am uncertain. I realised that true spirituality must be lived, not merely spoken. The Sa’i — walking between the hills of Safa and Marwah — touched me differently. It recalls the story of Hajar, who searched desperately for water for her infant son in the desert. Her story taught me that tawakkul, or trust in Allah, does not mean passivity. Her footsteps reflected both effort and complete trust in Allah. I thought about the person I had been, the person I had become and the person I still hoped to be. I remembered the blessings I had taken for granted and the countless ways Allah had been merciful to me despite my shortcomings. That thought changed the way I looked at my worldly ambitions. I do not believe Hajj taught me to abandon the world. It taught me not to let the world possess my heart. Standing among thousands of pilgrims also softened my understanding of others. I realised how little I knew about the struggles carried by those around me: the elderly person walking slowly, the exhausted mother carrying her child, and the person quietly making du’a — a personal prayer to God. Returning home was bittersweet. The physical journey was over, but the real question was beginning: What will remain when the memories fade? It is easy to be spiritual in Makkah. It is harder to preserve that spirituality in ordinary life. It is easy to cry during worship; it is harder to overcome contempt. It is easy to make promises to Allah in sacred places; it is harder to keep them when life becomes comfortable again. That, I believe, is the true test of Hajj.



When I think of Hajj now, I remember the Kaaba, the crowds, the heat, the prayers and the long walks. I remember the humility of ihram, the movement of Tawaf and the transient nature of life. I remember that I am a traveller. Essan Dileri is a Rotary Peace Fellow, intercultural advisor and author of Raised in Conflict, sharing first-hand stories from his native Afghanistan.

World.title: Forget Starbucks – welcome to the birthplace of China’s coffee industry
World.content:
WorldAsiaInside China Forget Starbucks – welcome to the birthplace of China’s coffee industry Lisa Visentin October 18, 2026 — 9:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Yunnan, China: On a remote mountain slope in south-west China, bamboo trays of freshly picked red coffee cherries are drying in courtyards and on the rooftops of farmers’ homes in the tiny village of Zhukula. Much of the fruit has been harvested from trees planted next to an old church more than a century ago by French missionaries who brought Arabica saplings, along with Catholicism, across the border from Vietnam. The village’s nascent Christian conversion didn’t survive the religious purges of the Cultural Revolution, but the coffee trees are now recognised as the oldest in the country, making Zhukula the birthplace of China’s coffee cultivation. Coffee roasting practices have remained unchanged in the village for decades, with the beans toasted over high heat using a wood-fired oil drum and cast-iron work for more than an hour. In this corner of China, long days ploughing and harvesting the mountainside are book-ended by coffee, not tea.



“Ever since I was little, as far back as I can remember, there have been coffee trees growing all around here,” says Li Jinrong, 57, a third-generation coffee farmer. “We make coffee as soon as we get up in the morning, drink it, go out to work and then have another cup before dinner.” Li Jinrong’s wife removes freshly roasted coffee beans from the hot cast-iron wok. The village of Zhukula has just one road in and out for its 83 households, reachable only by driving for hours along slender hairpin bends that snake around a mountain range. Li invites us into his farmhouse after we poke our heads through an open doorway leading to his courtyard, drawn in by a striking mound of yellow corn cobs baking in the sun and a noisy cat.



His home is a modest three-storey brick structure, centred around an open-air communal room with a concrete-slab floor. One corner functions as a kitchen, with a rice cooker and a camping stove rigged up to a single power board looped around a nail in the wall, while a collection of mismatched plastic stools surrounds a basic dining table. In the courtyard, he empties a rice sack filled with green coffee beans – shelled from their cherry skins – into a wood-fired roasting pit, fashioned out of an oil drum and large cast-iron work. Loading With a cooking shovel, he continuously turns the beans, a process that takes more than an hour to achieve a deep roast. It might seem nostalgically authentic, but it’s a laborious task that modern coffee manufacturers long ago outsourced to roasting machines. While China’s surging taste for coffee helped drive global prices to record highs in 2025, few, if any, farmers in Zhukula have grown rich from coffee.



“We grow coffee beans to make a living, but coffee alone isn’t enough. The problem is that we don’t have much farmland here,” Li says. “Coffee consumption [in China] has increased, but our area is small, so sales are unstable.” A woman in Zhukula sorts freshly harvested coffee cherries in a woven bamboo tray. Until about a decade ago, Yunnan was more famous for its tea production. Today, the sprawling mountainous region produces almost all of China’s coffee beans, an industry that has boomed as cafe culture has exploded across the country. China still trails miles behind Europe and the United States in terms of global coffee consumption, accounting for just 3 per cent, but it’s the fast-growing market, rising 150 per cent over the past decade.



It’s big business, with large commercial farms harvesting thousands of tonnes of coffee beans each year. You can find Yunnan beans in speciality coffee shops around the world, Australia included. But today, most of the region’s produce is consumed domestically, fuelled by the rapid expansion of coffee chains such as Chinese giant Luckin Coffee, which has opened 30,000 stores across the mainland since its first in Beijing in 2017. Boutique cafes serving oat milk lattes, iced Americanos and various berry infused, caramel-lashed, pistachio-rimmed concoctions are now abundant across Shanghai, Beijing and other major cities. This growing demand has helped pull farmers out of poverty in rural Yunnan, which remains one of China’s poorest provinces. The industry’s rise is also a case study in China’s 1980s pivot from a wholly planned economy to state-supported private enterprise and land cultivation, while also highlighting how rural land reform continues to constrain small-scale farmers.



Which boats have been lifted highest by this rising tide has depended heavily on geographical luck and the Communist Party’s “visible hand” in picking industrial and agricultural winners. Capitalism with Chinese characteristics Gao Jianyun, 63, chairman of Gaosheng Coffee, a company he built from his family’s farm in Baoshan in China’s Yunnan province. About half a day’s drive from Zhukula, towards China’s border with Myanmar, the sweeping valleys of Baoshan are blanketed in coffee trees, popping with red fruit. Many of them are owned by private commercial farms such as Gaosheng Coffee Manor, a family operated estate that runs a cafe, cupping room and tasting courses, while its German-imported industrial roasters churn through thousands of kilograms of beans each week.



Once an export-oriented business that used to count Nestlé and Starbucks as its largest clients, Gaosheng is now almost entirely focused on China’s domestic market. Related Article Inside China The Beijing pigeons that circle Mao before flying home “Luckin Coffee, Cotti Coffee and Mixue are our biggest customers. They’re our gods,” Gaosheng Coffee chairman Gao Jianyun says. The company is one of several large coffee enterprises that have sprung up in Baoshan over the past two decades. Its roots trace back to a 1950s state policy designating the region as one of China’s agricultural engine rooms, where farmers were instructed to grow coffee. “At that time, planting coffee wasn’t something they wanted to do themselves. It was mandated by the state’s planned economy,” says Gao, whose parents were among the first coffee farmers in the area.



Similar to the Li family in Zhukula, the Gao family also has three generations rooted in coffee farming, but their trajectories couldn’t be starker. As China’s economy opened up, and the government poured resources into making Baoshan a coffee cultivation powerhouse, the Gaos scaled up and invested in modern equipment, whereas the Zhukula farmers today remain limited by isolation, difficult terrain and low-earning capacity. When Gao joined his parents working on their farm in the early 1980s, all fresh coffee cherries were still purchased centrally by the collective, and his role was to calculate and distribute wages based on farmers’ planting area. Workers sort through green coffee beans, removing the flawed ones, at Gaosheng Coffee in Yunnan province, China. Luorui Xiang By 2005, the family had set up its own company, which today owns 34 hectares of coffee plants in Boashan and 80 hectares in the nearby Pu’er region and employs 100 people. Under China’s rural land system, farmers cannot buy or sell farmland, but they can lease their land-use rights to others, enabling wealthier operators and co-operatives to turn fragmented plots into larger estates. Gao says these farmers’ incomes have increased several times over. Meanwhile, Gaosheng Coffee is on track to make 120 million yuan ($26 million) this year through sales of green beans and packaged coffee products.



In the company’s boardroom, an airbrushed portrait of Chinese President Xi Jinping hangs on the wall, mounted alongside various golden plaques and accolades the business has been awarded. It’s a nod to the link between private commercial success and state support – particularly in the agriculture sector – under China’s model of “socialism with Chinese characteristics”. “We are also actively working with the government to expand our operations and increase production capacity,” Gao says. His daughter, Gao Jie, who studied a master of business administration in New York and now heads the company’s brand strategy, is aiming for a 20 per cent increase in sales this year. Some villagers in Zhukula keep small numbers of livestock in pens next to their farmhouses. Coffee farming frozen in time Back in Zhukula, the remote, rugged beauty of the mountain is also the farmers’ curse – a paradox familiar across rural China. Li’s house is the last at the end of the village, where the road abruptly gives way to a sheer drop to the valley and the Yupao River that flows through it.



The path to Li’s house is too narrow for cars and too steep for bicycles. It winds past his neighbours’ homes, where a few pigs, goats, cows and chickens are kept in cramped wooden pens next to their living quarters. It’s a portrait of communist agrarianism frozen in time, with faded Communist Party slogans painted in red on the outside of homes, urging villagers to march together towards prosperity. “Contentment with poverty is shameful. Overcoming poverty is honourable,” one slogan reads. A goat pokes its head through a window in a farmhouse stable in Zhukula village. A Communist Party slogan painted on the wall warns about “dark and evil forces”, a reference to organised crime. Luorui Xiang There’s a party activities centre in the village, while a few houses fly the hammer and sickle flag out front, identifying local members with leadership roles in the community. It’s indicative of how party governance is woven into the fabric of even China’s smallest villages. In the 1980s, after China abandoned the Mao-era commune and collective farming system, Li’s family was assigned 36 coffee trees under a policy that allocated land based on family size. Since then, it has expanded its coffee crop while also farming walnuts, Sichuan pepper and corn, but scaling up remains impossible on a plot of less than a hectare.



Higher bean prices have boosted the family’s income, but it’s still in the realm of subsistence rather than wealth generation. In a good year, Li and his 34-year-old son, Jiangfu – who also lives in the village with his wife and young daughter – harvest just under 1000 kilograms of coffee cherries. A Zhukula villager with fresh coffee cherries. The crop is the main source of each household’s annual income of about 25,000 yuan ($5400) – in line with the national average for rural farmers, but less than half what a migrant worker can earn as a delivery driver in Beijing or Shanghai. “Sales have gradually improved. In the past, many people didn’t know about our coffee, and it was difficult to sell,” Jiangfu says.



Now there’s a reliable stream of coffee shop owners, tourists and farmers’ friends and relatives who buy their beans, with demand outpacing their supplies, he says. Related Article China relations ‘Work is getting harder and harder to find’: On the street with China’s gig workers The village has clearly benefited from government efforts to transform it into a tourist destination, with newly paved roads, community toilet facilities and the church converted into a museum that chronicles Zhukula’s legacy as China’s first coffee village. A number of Li’s neighbours are building new homes and Li himself has partially renovated his house, with the support of government subsidies. Still, it is a world away from where some of Zhukula’s beans end up, served in trendy urban cafes as flat whites or experimental signature drinks for $10 a cup, alongside tasting notes exhorting the rich, nutty flavour of Yunnan coffee. World.title: How this relentless Australian bowling attack stacks up against the greats
World.content:
SportCricketAustralian cricket How this relentless Australian bowling attack stacks up against the greats Greg Chappell October 18, 2026 — 9:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Australia’s Test bowling attack ranks among the best in the world over the last 50 years, having broken new ground as a quartet and taking an unprecedented number of wickets as a four-man unit. Statistically, Pat Cummins, Mitchell Starc, Josh Hazlewood and Nathan Lyon sit comfortably in the same pantheon as some of the best West Indian attacks from the late ’70s. Loading Michael Holding, Andy Roberts, Joel Garner, Malcolm Marshall and Colin Croft combined hostility with control. People have described facing them as like facing an execution squad, offering no respite from either end. In Durban against South Africa last week, Australia out-bowled, out-batted and out-fielded their opponents and deserved their decisive victory. Central to the win was the attack.



Like past combinations from the late 1990s and early 2000s – comprising Glenn McGrath, Shane Warne, Jason Gillespie and Brett Lee – today’s attack offers the ultimate balance of precision, elite spin, pace and nagging persistence. The South African quartet of Dale Steyn, Morne Morkel, Vernon Philander, and Jacques Kallis from the late 2000s and mid-2010s also dominated an era favouring batting. Australian batsman Bruce Laird is struck on the hand by a Michael Holding delivery in 1980. Fairfax Media Then there was Pakistan’s outstanding attack: Imran Khan, Wasim Akram and Waqar Younis, with the spin of Abdul Qadir, another brilliant group who turned the old ball into lethal weapons capable of tearing through middle orders. Like the great West Indian combinations of the late 20th century and the Australian attack of the early 2000s, Cummins’ men thrive on discipline.



Hazlewood mirrors McGrath’s relentless probing line; Cummins attacks the stumps with fuller lengths; Starc provides the left-arm angle, swing, and X-factor pace; Lyon provides the control and sustained pressure of an elite spinner. While the historic West Indian pace battery holds the crown for sheer terror, and the 2000s Australian attack for ultimate match-winning balance, this crop matches them in longevity, relentless line and length and the ability to consistently grind down opponents through partnership bowling. In Kingsmead, batsman Matt Renshaw set the tone for Australia in the first innings with support from Cummins and Lyon. The desperation to post as high a score as possible from 6-124 on a challenging wicket was obvious. On his return to Test cricket, Nic Maddinson looked so desperate not to get out in the first innings that he made scoring look impossible. He soaked up much of the strike, and his dismissal was almost a relief to him.



Marnus Labuschagne looked more intent on scoring, and his resulting footwork was crisper. We may yet see the real Labuschagne by the end of the series. The real Steve Smith, meanwhile, is never far away. His dismissal soon after lunch on the first day, though, surprised everyone. South Africa didn’t bowl badly, but they didn’t bowl enough good balls in clumps to put pressure on the middle order on a wicket that was offering bounce. South Africa’s spinners were disappointing. They didn’t bowl a line or length suited to the conditions, so the Australians scored easily. Josh Hazlewood and skipper Pat Cummins form half of the most fearsome bowling quartet in Test cricket today. AP Photo/Themba Hadebe Renshaw was a tremendous success in the middle order. His game against spin worked in the conditions. This part of his game has developed in recent years. With his sweeping, he is ambidextrous and drove the spinners to distraction by carefully choosing his shots. He doesn’t try to over-hit his sweeps, relying on timing and placement to taunt the bowlers. He is a big man and uses his reach to advantage. Cummins could easily have been a genuine all-rounder if his bowling hadn’t demanded so much. He has a solid defence and an abundance of power. He was determined to lead by example, and his partnership with Renshaw was critical to the match.



Lyon is a fierce competitor who has become a better-than-useful tail-ender, handling short balls with the aplomb of a higher-rated batter. He is the perfect foil for a batter in this situation. His defence is solid; he is fearless and rotates the strike well. The Australians again gave a masterclass in bowling in any conditions through immaculate lines and lengths. Few have matched their ability to bowl together for extended periods. It must be like water torture to bat against them. Cummins is a class act. His return from injury to bowl at an elite pace, full and at the stumps, is exceptional. He consistently directs his bouncer with precision and utilises it efficiently, seldom wasting it. His default length is fuller than most, so every ball demands a response, and his full-blooded attack demands wickets. He is inspiring. Starc looked a little rusty, but that is the beauty of this group. If one doesn’t get you, someone else will. Hazlewood was brilliant. His line rarely changes, and he bowls a suffocating length. It must feel as if you are batting against a boa constrictor. It is only a matter of how long it takes for him to squeeze the life out of you.



Hazlewood and Lyon have returned from serious injuries and have resumed business as usual. Their professionalism showed in how wholeheartedly they committed to their rehabilitation. Related Article Australian cricket Reversal of fortune: Hazlewood says old-ball swing ‘crucial’ to South Africa triumph Lyon showed his opposition spinners how to bowl in the conditions. His line, length, and pace were ideal, and his relentlessness was top-class. The opposition spinners gave the Australians too much room, which let the pressure off too often. Lyon’s pace, with maximum revs and line, is much harder to reverse-sweep than his two opposition spinners. The second-innings situation gave Maddinson some freedom, and he looked like a different player. Had he been more fortunate with the timing of his earlier selection, he could easily have played much more Test cricket.



Australia got some luck in this Test because South Africa were without their two best pace bowlers, Kagiso Rabada and Lungi Ngidi. Had Rabada played, the outcome could have been very different. His absence was deeply felt, and the Proteas will need him for the rest of the series to change the result. With Steve Smith passing the concussion tests, he will play in the second Test. That is a bonus for Australia, as he remains the group’s most reliable batter. His batting is key for Australia, and so is his brilliant fielding. Australia would not want to lose him. The bowling attack and Steve Smith are still critical to the side’s success.

World.title: King Dobby ate a Croc and a bottle top – leaving his owners an impossible $6000 choice
World.content:
NationalVictoriaPets King Dobby ate a Croc and a bottle top – leaving his owners an impossible $6000 choice James Costa October 18, 2026 — 8:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. “King” Dobby, as the Chihuahua Dachshund cross is called, wasn’t behaving like his normal, energy-filled and demanding self. He wasn’t playing, he was lethargic, and sat shaking on the corner of the bed – usually he’s plonked right in the middle of his owners. His family knew something was wrong and rushed him to the Lort Smith Animal Hospital. Dobby, the Chihuahua Dachshund cross, had to be rushed to the animal hospital after eating a Croc and bottletop. Ruby Alexander Turns out he had eaten an olive oil bottle top and chewed up a Croc sandal. The emergency surgery, necessary for the life-threatening blockage, was set to cost them almost $6000. The Aarons family – Caitlin, Jai and their two sons – were distraught. They couldn’t afford the massive vet bill and had to stop and contemplate letting Dobby go.



“[I was] feeling lower than crap because, like, I can’t afford to get my fur baby fixed,” said Caitlin. How on earth, she thought, would she tell her kids their dog wouldn’t be coming home? The Aarons are not alone. Across Victoria, families are skipping vet visits, missing out on preventative care and, increasingly, facing the difficult decision of either incurring debt or euthanising their pet. A 2025 survey by Animal Medicines Australia, the peak body representing the animal health industry, found that about 16 per cent of pet owners had accessed financial assistance to cover the cost of veterinary care, and that one in six people skipped taking their dog or cat to the vet to save money. Last year, 54 per cent of all people who visited pet hospital Lort Smith were struggling financially and received discounted care from the not-for-profit.



“Financially, it was incredibly stressful,” Caitlin said. “It was the day before payday, we don’t have pet insurance, and we couldn’t use Afterpay. I had to borrow money from family just to get started. I was panicking, wondering what we were going to do and calling everyone for help.” Caitlin, Jai, Laurence and James Aarons with their dog, Dobby. Ruby Alexander After much stress, Dobby got the surgery he needed. Lort Smith has a fund for people experiencing financial hardship. That fund, said Caitlin, covered almost $4000 for the surgery, with the family borrowing the remaining $2000 with a no-interest loan from Good Shepherd. “I was so worried about paying for treatment that I couldn’t even food shop,” Caitlin said. “We were just eating whatever was left in the fridge, hoping for the best but preparing for the worst.” Lort Smith chief executive Frances Mirabelli said the hospital is eating into its cash reserves to keep pace with rising costs and surging demand for its care.



To manage the volume, Mirabelli has rostered extra vets, staff and volunteers. But the model relies heavily on full-paying clients to subsidise care for those who cannot afford it – a balance that is becoming harder to maintain as household budgets tighten across the state. With a state election approaching, the hospital is calling on both the government and the opposition to commit $1 million in targeted funding. “That’d help us help thousands of animals, and have a massive impact on so many people,” Mirabelli said. Lort Smith Animal Hospital chief executive Frances Mirabelli. Simon Schluter “It’s the emergencies that are the problem,” Mirabelli said, “that’s when it starts get really expensive. That’s not because we’re making huge profits – it’s just because that’s the cost of care at the moment.” Beyond that emergency relief, Lort Smith is also seeking an additional $4 million commitment to expand its crisis relief animal boarding network for the pets of people experiencing family violence.

World.title: The leap second has been cancelled. It’s about time
World.content:
WorldEuropeDaylight saving The leap second has been cancelled. It’s about time K.R. Callaway October 18, 2026 — 8:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Every few years since 1972, computers, financial institutions, communications networks and other systems have had to reset their clocks by a single second. On Thursday, the international authority on timekeeping voted to abolish this contentious quirk of global synchronisation. The change will take effect in 2027. In a meeting of officials from the International Bureau of Weights and Measures, or BIPM, in France, the group axed the leap second, which had been established to align our clocks with Earth’s rotation. The practice was similar to that of the leap year, when an extra day is added to our calendars to keep us in sync with Earth’s orbit around the sun. Leap years are predictable, happening every four years. But leap seconds account for seemingly random irregularities in how fast Earth rotates, which has been causing trouble for timekeepers, including the looming possibility of needing a “negative leap second” because Earth’s spin is getting faster. Michael Wouters from the CSIRO with Australia’s atomic clock. Ben Rushton “This decision has become particularly timely because recent changes in the Earth’s rotation have raised the possibility of a first-ever negative leap second, which has never been experienced and that could create additional risks for critical infrastructures,” Noel Dimarcq, president of the BIPM’s committee for time and frequency, said in a statement.



In lieu of the added second, humankind will wait until an entire hour is needed to bring us back into synchronisation with the planet’s spin. This new practice is “just easier” to keep track of, said Patrizia Tavella, director of the bureau’s time department. Related Article Explainer

Daylight saving It’s daylight saving time again – but why do we have it at all? It’s unclear when this extra hour may be needed, but it might not happen for centuries. “It’s really just taking the problem well, well into the future,” said Andrew Novick, an electrical engineer and manager of the time and frequency division at the National Institute of Standards and Technology, or NIST, in Maryland. “It could be thousands of years before this leap hour happens.” For much of history, “the Earth was the best available clock”, Duncan Agnew, a geophysicist at Scripps Institution of Oceanography in California, explained during the meeting. Keeping time mostly involved ways of dividing how long it takes Earth to complete one rotation on its axis: Earth rotates at about 1000 mp/h (1600 km/h) on average, so a day equals 86,400 seconds.



By the mid-20th century, humans needed more timekeeping precision to support the advent of computers, international communications systems and space exploration. Enter atomic clocks, which measure time by tracking the tiny changes atoms undergo at regular intervals. These ultra-precise clocks ushered in a global way of keeping time: Coordinated Universal Time, or UTC, which was adopted in 1963. “You only know how good your clock is when you get a better clock,” Novick said. Sometimes gravitational interactions with other celestial bodies or the movements of air, water and rock on our dynamic planet can affect its rotation speed. Once clocks became more precise, these subtle shifts in Earth’s rotation became more noticeable, which is why we adopted the leap second. In recent decades, though, the added second posed two main problems for our digital systems. For starters, it can be a hassle to change the time by a single second and could even cause time-linked systems to temporarily shut down. Some tech giants such as Google adopted a “leap smear” instead, temporarily slowing down their clocks rather than adding the leap. What’s more, Earth’s rotation isn’t always lagging behind. The same forces that slow it down can also work in reverse, meaning that one day we might have a negative leap second. And while most of the digital systems that rely on UTC are prepared to jump ahead, far fewer have the code built in to handle a move backward in time.



The Earth has rotated on its axis at roughly 15 degrees an hour for about 4.6 billion years. Time zones, on the other hand, are an extremely recent human creation. Adobe Stock Since the 2000s, Earth’s rotation has been speeding up, driven by a combination of changes to Earth’s core and surface phenomena like the melting polar ice caps. This makes the need for a negative leap second more likely, and, in part, drove timekeepers to their decision to end the leap second. Related Article Explainer

Science Why do we have leap years (and what does Cleopatra have to do with them)? The vote was not unanimous. Delegates from Russia, whose satellites often have a built-in system for handling leap seconds, voted against the measure, and those from Belarus abstained. The differential between our clocks and Earth’s rotation is currently hovering around zero, meaning the next leap second could have easily been a negative one, Novick said. Still, Novick and other scientists said they will miss this little idiosyncrasy in the way we keep time.



“It’s the one time you could almost assure that NIST would be on the news,” Novick said, “because it gets people thinking about the Earth’s rotation, and about time.” This article originally appeared in The New York Times. World.content:
Updated NationalNSWCrime Teen, 13, charged as police investigate alleged sex offences on walking trails Sarah McPhee and Michaela Whitbourn Updated October 18, 2026 — 6:30am ,first published October 17, 2026 — 7:14am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Police have charged a teenager over multiple sexual offences allegedly committed against women on walking trails in Sydney’s northern beaches. “Following a public appeal, a 13-year-old boy was arrested after attending Mona Vale police station about 7.30pm,” NSW Police said in a statement on Saturday. Several women have reported sexual touching and harassment on the Narrabeen Lagoon trail over the past week. Internet He was charged overnight with three counts of behaving in an offensive manner near a public place and eight counts of sexually touching another person without consent. Police will allege that there were 11 separate incidents involving women and girls aged between 13 and 54 in the Narrabeen area, mostly between October 1 and 12.



Related Article Crime Multiple women allegedly targeted on northern beaches walking trails There was also an earlier incident, where a woman was allegedly spoken to inappropriately at the intersection of Waroon Road and Carawa Road, Cromer, about 6.45pm on September 7. Investigations began after three alleged incidents in two days, during which “a male allegedly approached women on walking trails, sexually touched them and then rode away on an e-bike”, police said. “In one of the incidents, the man also [allegedly] made inappropriate sexual comments.” Another woman came forward alleging that at the start of the month, she was sexually touched by a man at Narrabeen Lagoon and that he then rode away on an e-bike.



Two women further reported they had been sexually touched by a male riding an e-bike on October 12 as they walked along the lagoon near Bilarong Reserve. The teenager has been granted conditional bail to appear in a children’s court on November 4. Anyone with information, mobile phone or dashcam footage, or who may have witnessed any of the incidents is urged to contact Crime Stoppers on 1800 333 000. World.title: ‘Planned operation’: The test result that reveals a dangerous Trump betrayal
World.content:
Analysis WorldEuropeRussia-Ukraine war ‘Planned operation’: The test result that reveals a dangerous Trump betrayal David Crowe October 18, 2026 — 5:55am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. London: A satellite speed test on a European motorway is an unusual way to check whether Donald Trump can be trusted. But the test results are impossible to ignore when they challenge everything the American president claims about the war in Ukraine. The results also have implications for every American ally when the findings suggest the Trump administration has slowed the speed of the Starlink satellite network, and its Starshield military system, so Ukrainian targets are more exposed to Russian attacks. Donald Trump and Elon Musk pictured outside the White House in August. AP Just think of the gravity of that decision. All the signs suggest the Americans made a technical change that increased civilian casualties. Without Starlink working properly, Ukrainian drones lost the power to intercept Russian drones. The rational conclusion is that civilians died from a decision in Washington DC to limit the use of an American network.



The speed test was undertaken in recent days by Ukrainian personnel who took Starlink equipment into a nearby European Union country to check whether they would get the same slow speeds they experienced when using the terminals in Ukraine. Related Article Russia-Ukraine war Musk approached Trump to slow down Starlink in Ukraine The result? Starlink worked for vehicles travelling at 180km/h in Europe. In Ukraine, however, service was cut out for drones travelling at more than 161km/h. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky revealed the results to journalists on Saturday (Sunday AEDT) and explained why they mattered. When Ukrainian forces send a drone to intercept a Russian attack, he said, they “lose the drone” when it travels at a speed higher than the Starlink cap. While they could slow the drone, of course, that would only make it harder to intercept a Russian kamikaze drone heading for an apartment building.



Zelensky concluded that the technical limit on Starlink in Ukraine was no accident. “Limitations are in effect on the territory of Ukraine, and limitations are not in effect on the territory of the EU countries,” he said. “That is, this is a planned operation.” So, who planned it? This is a question every American ally, including Australia, should want answered. Trump denies being responsible and also tries to protect Elon Musk, the founder and controller of Starlink and its parent company, SpaceX. “It wasn’t me and I don’t think it was Elon,” he said on Friday.



Well, somebody in the Trump administration did it. The Telegraph reported on Friday that Musk suggested the move to Trump, who liked the idea. Reuters reported the order came from inside the White House. Trump claims he wants peace in Ukraine, but his latest decisions have the effect of helping Russia wage war. He has blocked funding for Ukraine, limited its access to Patriot interceptors, hedged on a security guarantee in any ceasefire and suggested Zelensky should cede more territory to Putin. He is also unwinding sanctions against Russia, starting with a deal to let the Kremlin make more money from diesel fuel exports. Loading “It’s immoral and it makes no sense,” the former US ambassador to Russia, Michael McFaul, said of the diesel and sanctions moves on US television. “What American national interest is advanced by these decisions? There’s none.” Australians should be watching this closely. Remember, it was only 18 months ago that Trump talked of having a way to limit the features of jet fighters used by allies. This “kill switch” talk alarmed the US defence industry, which feared it would lose sales.



Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney is responding carefully to what Trump says. He has started a review of a Canadian plan to buy a fleet of F-35 stealth fighters from the US. Canada has also gained “observer” status on a sixth-generation fighter being developed by the UK, Italy and Japan. Related Article Updated

Russia-Ukraine war ‘Betrayed’: Ukraine leader denounces Trump for siding with Russia amid row with Musk At a time when Australia is committed to buying US submarines under the AUKUS program, it is essential to confront the inherent risk in relying on the US under Trump. It is no longer science fiction to think that someone in Washington DC might want to “switch off” the military capability of an ally. Ukraine is not a formal US ally. Until Trump, however, it was promised full support from America under security agreements. Former president Joe Biden hedged on shipping some of the armaments Zelensky wanted, but he kept funding Ukraine to try to stop Russia because this was seen as vital to the interest of the US and its NATO allies. Yes, the head-spinning shift under Trump betrays Ukraine. But it does more than this. It warns all American partners of the danger of depending on an unreliable ally.



European leaders, like those in Australia, are extremely wary of offending Trump by directly criticising his decisions to help Putin. Their approach is to use optics, like the social media clips of their warm meetings with Zelensky, to show where they stand. Zelensky has a very different objective. He has acted to maximise attention on the American decision on Starlink speeds. The effect is to highlight the questions about Trump’s judgment, even if Zelensky risks an even greater rupture in his relationship with the president. What else can Zelensky do? There seems to be no benefit to Ukraine in staying quiet, so Zelensky seeks to make sure that Americans know what Trump has done. World.title: What my pilgrimage to Mecca taught me
World.content:
LifestyleLife & relationshipsReligion Opinion What my pilgrimage to Mecca taught me

Essan Dileri October 18, 2026 — 5:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

While on the journey to perform Hajj, the Muslim pilgrimage to Makkah (Mecca), I realised that Hajj was asking something much deeper of me. It was asking me to leave behind not only my home and possessions, but also my pride, attachments, fears and illusions of control. Essan Dileri in front of the Kaaba, in Mecca, as he does his hajj. Photo: Supplied When I entered ihram — the sacred state pilgrims enter, symbolised by simple clothing — I felt that something within me was being stripped away. The distinctions by which I sometimes measure myself seemed to lose meaning. I noticed that my nationality, education, appearance and social position became insignificant. I found myself standing before Allah (God) dressed simply, vulnerable and equal. The simplicity of ihram also made me think about the transience of this life. When I first saw the Kaaba, the sacred structure at the heart of the Grand Mosque in Makkah towards which Muslims around the world pray, I struggled to put my emotions into words. I had spent my life turning towards it in prayer, but suddenly I was standing before it. For a moment, the distance between what I had known intellectually and what I was experiencing spiritually disappeared. I felt small and humbled. I couldn’t stop crying. During Tawaf, the ritual of walking seven times around the Kaaba, I began to reflect on what occupies the centre of my life. I was physically circling the House of Allah, but inwardly I was asking myself: What does my heart revolve around? Is it Allah, or is it success, comfort, fear or the judgement of others?



That question stayed with me. Tawaf taught me that faith is not simply about where I turn my body during prayer. It is about where I turn my heart when I am scared and where I place my hopes when I am uncertain. I realised that true spirituality must be lived, not merely spoken. The Sa’i — walking between the hills of Safa and Marwah — touched me differently. It recalls the story of Hajar, who searched desperately for water for her infant son in the desert. Her story taught me that tawakkul, or trust in Allah, does not mean passivity. Her footsteps reflected both effort and complete trust in Allah. I thought about the person I had been, the person I had become and the person I still hoped to be. I remembered the blessings I had taken for granted and the countless ways Allah had been merciful to me despite my shortcomings. That thought changed the way I looked at my worldly ambitions. I do not believe Hajj taught me to abandon the world. It taught me not to let the world possess my heart. Standing among thousands of pilgrims also softened my understanding of others. I realised how little I knew about the struggles carried by those around me: the elderly person walking slowly, the exhausted mother carrying her child, and the person quietly making du’a — a personal prayer to God. Returning home was bittersweet. The physical journey was over, but the real question was beginning: What will remain when the memories fade? It is easy to be spiritual in Makkah. It is harder to preserve that spirituality in ordinary life. It is easy to cry during worship; it is harder to overcome contempt. It is easy to make promises to Allah in sacred places; it is harder to keep them when life becomes comfortable again. That, I believe, is the true test of Hajj.



When I think of Hajj now, I remember the Kaaba, the crowds, the heat, the prayers and the long walks. I remember the humility of ihram, the movement of Tawaf and the transient nature of life. I remember that I am a traveller. Essan Dileri is a Rotary Peace Fellow, intercultural advisor and author of Raised in Conflict, sharing first-hand stories from his native Afghanistan.

World.title: Election 2026: National promises removing right to silence in child murder cases
World.content: Follow our daily live coverage of all the happening on the 2026 election campaign trail. We'll have updates, breaking news and analysis from Political Editor Jo Moir, Deputy Editor Craig McCulloch and their team through to election day on 7 November.

World.title: National pledges to take away right to silence when a child is murdered
World.content:
National says it will take away a person's right to silence when a child is murdered if the party is re-elected.

Justice spokesperson Paul Goldsmith announced this morning that the party would make it a Crimes Act offence not to disclose information to police when a person has been present the location where a child under 12 has been killed.

"It will apply when a child under 12 dies, and at the time of death, or leading up to the death, it is unequivocal that one or more adults were present," Goldsmith said.

This would carry a maximum sentence of 10 years in prison.

"Too many children in New Zealand die at the hands of, or with the knowledge of, people who should be protecting them. The right to silence should not be abused to the extent that these horrific crimes go unpunished," Goldsmith said.

World.title: Prime Minister passed over easier election dates, advice reveals
World.content:
Prime Minister Christopher Luxon picked a "challenging" election date, despite the Electoral Commission favouring two other options, newly released advice shows.

Labour is accusing Luxon of "knowingly limiting turnout" by putting up another barrier to voting.

Advice seen by RNZ shows the commission described the chosen date of 7 November as "challenging, but manageable", partly because advance voting would begin on a public holiday.

Two alternatives - 17 October and 21 November - around that time were considered "administratively more feasible".

A range of dates in August and September were also more feasible.

In a letter to the prime minister on 7 August 2025, the chief electoral officer warned that school and public holidays could see large numbers of voters away from home, potentially reducing voter turnout.

"Our practice has been to advise on avoiding an election date during these times."

Labour is also concerned there'll be fewer voting booths open on the public holiday.

When Luxon announced the election date in January, he described it as the "logical time", after weighing up sporting fixtures and other events. He noted that eight of the last 12 elections were also held in October or November.

Labour MP Camilla Belich questioned that logic, saying the prime minister had other options that would have avoided the Labour Day clash.

Camilla Belich worries Epsom voters will find polling booths closed on Labour Day. VNP/Phil Smith

She said just two of the 22 voting places in Epsom, the electorate she is contesting, would be open on 26 October and voters could turn up to cast their ballot, only to find the booth closed.

RNZ suggested to Belich that Labour Day was just one day in a 13-day voting period. She acknowledged the impact might be limited, but argued that even a small number of voters being inconvenienced mattered in a tight election.

"Every vote is going to count," she said. "This is another barrier, really."

Belich said the decision was compounded by the government's earlier changes to electoral law, scrapping same-day voter enrolment.

The National Party has dismissed Labour's criticism as a sign of desperation, pointing out the election date had been public knowledge for nine months.

A party spokesperson suggested Labour leader Chris Hipkins must be "very worried" about his campaign to be raising the matter now.
